chapters.title: Build Radically Candid Relationships
chapters.hook: The advice was right. Everyone agreed, but the person who needed it heard blame.
chapters.counterintuition: Care does not slow candor; it gives candor somewhere to land. A direct view heard from someone who has noticed you can sound like help.
chapters.tryThisNow: Count one current conversation: write the number of visible care signals already present before any hard sentence. Capture only that number.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Count visible care before direct guidance: when concern is already real and seen, a hard view can land as help instead of rank, attack, or distance.

breakdown.fastRead:
The advice can be right and still miss. A person leaves with the standard in their ears and no reason to hear it as help.

Kim Scott, a former Google executive tied to Google AdSense, gives the idea its live setting. Her later Apple role adds another place where the count matters. This is not nicer wording: has the other person seen that you know they are more than output?

Radical Candor joins Care Personally, seeing the whole person, with Challenge Directly, naming strong output and output that falls short. Count the care before the challenge. Then offer the view as a view, not as owned truth.
breakdown.deepRead:
Care lowers the guard that rises when a person feels judged from far away. The direct line may still sting, but visible concern gives the person a reason to hear the sting as help.

Here is the guardrail. Do not use care as a warm cover for a blow you have already decided to land. Do not ask for private pain that is not yours to hear. If the fact must be said now, say it plainly and leave room for reply.

Professional means clear and human at once. Care Personally can be small: noticing a bad day or making space for someone to say the day is rough. It can also mean dropping the robot pose long enough to show there is a person on both sides of the talk.

Sheryl Sandberg, the Google leader later tied to Facebook and a 2017 public example of human leadership, shows the care side without making it soft. Public accounts present her style as rooted in human ties on the job. The useful part is not drama. A small sign of humanity can shorten awkward silence, so people can return to hard business questions with less pretending.

What has the person already seen? That question comes before the hard sentence. If they have seen only distance, your direct view has to carry too much weight. If they have seen care, the same view has a doorway.

Care does not soften truth; it gives truth a human door. The door still needs the other half: Challenge Directly. Say what is strong. Say where output falls short. Then hold the sentence humbly, as your view, so correction can come back through the same door.
breakdown.fullRead:
The compass is useful only when it stays on the exchange in front of you. It is not a stamp for a kind of person. A person can move by behavior, so the better question is, what showed up here?

The Care Personally plus Challenge Directly compass, the public two-axis map for these talks, names four zones. Radical Candor means care and challenge together. Obnoxious Aggression means bluntness without care. Ruinous Empathy means warmth without the needed challenge. Manipulative Insincerity means neither clear care nor clear challenge.

Labels get dangerous fast. If you call a colleague candid as a fixed identity, you may excuse rough conduct. If you call someone aggressive as a fixed identity, you may miss the next repair. The compass should ask which side was absent in this exchange, then point to the behavior that would add it.

Kim Scott's Google AdSense and Apple executive settings keep the tool out of etiquette class. Google AdSense gives it a product and management setting. The Apple executive role gives it another operating setting. The proof is not that famous companies make a phrase true. The proof is that care and challenge have to survive speed, quality, and real people.

That setting also keeps directness honest. Challenge Directly covers praise and criticism, so clarity is not the same as negativity. If you name only weak output, people learn what failed but not what to repeat. If you praise without a standard, warmth floats away from the task.

Humility is the hinge on the direct side. Challenge Directly means sharing a view, not owning the truth. Can the other person correct you without paying a price? If not, your directness has become certainty with better branding.

The count travels sideways too. You may have no title. Before you challenge a peer, count whether they have seen you care about their load, their aim, or the risk they carry. Before you praise, make the standard clear enough to repeat. Before you criticize, make the view humble enough to answer.

Had Scott's Silicon Valley setting been treated as manners advice, the move would shrink. People would try to sound nicer while still waiting too long or striking too hard. Had the compass become a label for types, it would freeze people in the very boxes it was built to help them leave.

This move fails when care is staged at the last second. People notice when a warm line is used to soften a verdict. In that case, skip the performance. State the fact, state the standard, and make room for reply. Care is evidence, not decoration.

A doorway is the image. Leave it shut, and even true words may sound like force. Open it with real concern, and direct guidance has a chance to be heard as help.

examples.title: After the Miss
examples.scenario: Picture a direct line missing under the pressure Kim Scott worked in as a manager: a former Google executive on Google AdSense, later in an Apple executive role. No private hallway scene exists to replay, so treat the miss as a thought experiment, not a biography. Run the trace: had care not been visible before the line, accuracy would have had to carry the doorway by itself.
examples.whatToDo: Work from the roles, not an imagined scene. Count whether concern was visible before the line was said, then restate the hard view as a view.
examples.whyItMatters: Without the count, Google AdSense and Apple become prestige stamps. The skipped care signal leaves directness to sound like rank, even when the content is right.

examples.title: The Shorter Silence
examples.scenario: Sheryl Sandberg's public example reaches people downstream before anyone names a framework. As a Google leader later tied to Facebook and a 2017 public example of human leadership, she is used to show visible vulnerability on the job. The move half-works: awkward silence gets shorter, but openness alone still does not name what high standards require.
examples.whatToDo: A small human signal works because it cuts the pretending. Then return to the hard business question, so care opens the door instead of replacing the standard.
examples.whyItMatters: Skip that return and the move stays half-finished. Vulnerability is not anti-performance; it earns room for demanding words but cannot supply them alone.

examples.title: Zero Praise Count
examples.scenario: During a guidance audit, a manager finds zero as the number that does not add up: no specific praise beside the corrections. The Care Personally plus Challenge Directly compass names two axes, and Kim Scott's Google AdSense and Apple executive role keep those axes tied to live tasks. A pen stops at the blank line. The cost lands now: without praise, the standard teaches only what failed.
examples.whatToDo: What would you ask first? Ask what strong result should repeat, then name it as clearly as you would name a miss, with care for the person kept visible.
examples.whyItMatters: Skip praise and directness turns negative by habit. The person learns what failed, but not what to repeat, so the standard gets thinner instead of clearer.

examples.title: Drop the Label
examples.scenario: At the start of a follow-up call, a manager states the standard: do not use Radical Candor as brutal honesty. The miss is close: a rough exchange is about to become a fixed label for a colleague. The Care Personally plus Challenge Directly compass pulls it back. It reads the behavior in this exchange, then asks which side was absent.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the label. Name the missing side in the exchange, then add care or directness in the next behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: Fixed labels freeze repair. Moment diagnosis leaves the person movable and keeps bluntness from posing as candor.

questions.prompt: Your release note says the partner was wrong, and your proof feels solid before you send it to the launch group. Which next move best fits direct challenge?
choices: Send the note with the proof up front, so the partner sees that the call is settled before debate starts.
State your read plainly, mark it as a view, and invite correction on any fact you may have missed.
Hold the note until the partner agrees first, so humility does not risk a direct disagreement.
questions.explanation: Direct challenge is a humble view, not possession of truth. The proof-first move looks rigorous, but it closes the door that correction needs.

questions.prompt: A design lead praises a clean handoff but saves all corrections for later. Which choice best preserves direct challenge?
choices: Let the praise carry the standard for now, since criticism may feel sharper after a clean handoff.
Name the strong handoff and the weak spots, so clarity covers what to repeat and what to fix.
Keep the correction private until the next cycle, so the praise can stay clearly positive.
questions.explanation: Challenge Directly covers praise and criticism. Saving every correction makes directness sound negative, while vague praise fails to teach the repeatable standard.

questions.prompt: After a senior director admits the day is rough, the group gets less tense. What should happen if the move lands?
choices: The group can return to hard business questions with less pretending, while the standard still has to be named.
The group can treat the disclosure as enough guidance, since the human signal has reset the tone and lowered the pressure.
The group should wait for more personal sharing before it takes up the business question again and risks renewed tension.
questions.explanation: Visible humanity reduces awkward silence so the hard question can come back. Treating the disclosure as the full answer leaves the standard unspoken.

questions.prompt: During a rough morning, a colleague says they are not at their best, and the file still needs clear comments. What fits Care Personally?
choices: Turn the comment into a full personal debrief, since ordinary signals may be too thin for trust.
Move past the comment quickly, because professional care should stay outside the task.
Acknowledge the bad day and make room to continue, without pressing for a deeper disclosure.
questions.explanation: Small signals can show humanity. The full-debrief move waits for drama; the better move recognizes the person and keeps the task honest.

questions.prompt: Blunt counsel to a peer cannot wait past today, and you count no sign that they have seen you understand their load. What should you do?
choices: Skip the last-second warm-up, state the fact plainly as your read of the situation, and leave the peer clear room to reply.
Make one care signal visible right before the counsel, so the hard view arrives wrapped in fresh warmth.
Hold the counsel until real care signals have built up over time, since a zero count means the view cannot land yet.
questions.explanation: Care staged seconds before a verdict reads as performance, and people notice. When the count is zero and the fact cannot wait, the sound move is a plain view with room for reply. Real concern gets built before the next hard talk, not at the last second.

questions.prompt: Someone calls Radical Candor permission to be brutally honest in a product critique. What correction is strongest?
choices: Keep the harsh facts but add a friendly close, so the product critique has a warmer finish.
Separate candor from harsh delivery, since care changes how the same fact is received.
Use brutal honesty only with senior peers, who may value direct facts more than care.
questions.explanation: Brutal honesty lacks the care axis. A friendly close is tempting, but care is not a wrapper placed after harsh delivery.

questions.prompt: A peer splits one project handoff for kindness and another for honesty, hoping the balance will feel fair across the week. What breaks?
choices: The peer applies care too broadly, because a candid exchange should rely more on challenge than concern.
The peer applies challenge too narrowly, because kindness alone can be enough when the bond feels warm.
The peer separates the two axes, when the useful behavior needs care and challenge in the same exchange.
questions.explanation: Either axis alone distorts the exchange. The warm-bond answer is plausible, but warmth without challenge can still hide useful truth.

questions.prompt: Your colleague treats Kim Scott's Google and Apple background as branding for polite office behavior. What is the better read?
choices: The settings tie the idea to management pressure, products, and roles, not just etiquette.
The settings prove the idea fits mainly in famous technology companies with public leaders.
The settings are useful as biography, while the actual lesson should ignore operating context.
questions.explanation: Google AdSense and Apple ground the idea in operating roles. The famous-company answer uses the wrong proof: brand weight does not settle the mechanism.

questions.prompt: After a tense exchange, a supervisor labels a colleague aggressive while drafting a follow-up. Which follow-up uses the compass well?
choices: Keep the label for similar exchanges, since one strong example can help the supervisor spot the pattern before another tense follow-up.
Switch the label to candid if the colleague gives a useful fact later and sounds less harsh.
Ask which side was missing in that exchange, because the compass diagnoses behavior rather than identity.
questions.explanation: The compass reads moments, not fixed selves. Switching to a nicer label still brands the person; the better move asks what care or challenge was absent.

reviewCards.front: What has to be visible before direct guidance is more likely to land as help?
reviewCards.back: Whole-person concern has to be visible. The person needs evidence that you see more than output, so the hard sentence has a better chance of sounding helpful.

reviewCards.front: Why is direct challenge not the same as criticism?
reviewCards.back: It names strong output and output that is not good enough. Specific praise is part of the standard, because it tells someone what to repeat.

reviewCards.front: What goes wrong when kindness and honesty are split into separate styles?
reviewCards.back: One side goes missing. Kindness without challenge can hide useful truth, and honesty without care can sound like attack. The useful move joins both.

reviewCards.front: What should the compass diagnose?
reviewCards.back: It should diagnose the behavior in a conversation, not brand a person. Ask which side was missing, then add care or directness in the next behavior.

reviewCards.front: Why is brutal honesty outside Radical Candor?
reviewCards.back: Brutal honesty lacks the care side. The same fact can help or harm depending on whether concern is visible and the person has room to answer.

reviewCards.front: What keeps direct challenge from turning into certainty?
reviewCards.back: Humility. State the view clearly, but leave space for correction. You are offering a candid read, not claiming to own the truth.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Count Visible Care. Before direct guidance, count the signs the other person can see that you notice them as a whole person. Then state the view plainly and humbly, so they can correct what you missed.

ifThenPlans.context: A hard sentence is ready, and no recent care signal is visible.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the count is zero, then skip the last-second warm-up: give the hard view plainly as your read and leave room for reply; then show real care in the days after.

ifThenPlans.context: Praise is due, and the repeatable standard could stay vague.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the strong result could be repeated, then name the result plainly; then say what standard it proves.

ifThenPlans.context: One rough exchange is turning into a fixed label for a person.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the label appears, then count which side was missing in that exchange; then replace the label with one repair behavior.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Teach one person the move in your own words: count visible care before direct words. Use one live example and count the signal together.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, if a hard message is ready to send, then count visible care first and record the number beside the message.

memorableLines.text: Count the care before the challenge.
Care does not soften truth; it gives truth a human door.
Professional means clear and human at once.

chapters.title: Get, Give, and Encourage Guidance
chapters.hook: Who pays when kind silence keeps the one useful fact out of reach?
chapters.counterintuition: Niceness can become the costly move. If you hide the useful fact to save the moment, the person who needs it loses the chance to change.
chapters.tryThisNow: Ask one person in the next 10 minutes: "What did I do this week that made your task harder?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: Ask for criticism first, give praise and correction as specific facts, and help peers speak directly before comfort turns missing truth into lost time.

breakdown.fastRead:
Who pays if Sheryl Sandberg keeps the hard observation quiet? Sandberg keeps the calm minute for herself, and Kim Scott loses a fact she can use. Sandberg was the manager Scott answered to during their Google years, a story Scott made public in 2017, and that standing trust is why direct guidance can land as help instead of shame.

Ruinous Empathy means care without direct challenge. Put plainly, warmth hides the needed fact. That is the price. Guidance culture means praise and criticism move up, down, and across peers. Start by asking for criticism of your own behavior. Then give specific praise and correction. Then encourage feedback between team members, because the person who sees the problem first may not be the boss.
breakdown.deepRead:
The trap is comfort that looks kind. You skip the hard sentence, no one flinches, and the missing fact moves out of reach. Every hidden fact sends the bill to the person you meant to spare.

Sheryl Sandberg and Kim Scott show the cleaner version. Sandberg managed Scott at Google, and Scott told the story publicly in 2017. Trust already exists. Sandberg can make a hard observation, and Scott can hear it as help. The lesson is not to copy a sharp tone. The relationship is part of the mechanism.

Bob shows the failure. At Juice Software, delayed criticism led toward firing. First, Bob lacked the clear fact. Then the problem grew harder for everyone. Last, the real talk carried too much weight. Late truth no longer sounded like help. It sounded like a verdict.

The feedback order of operations keeps the cost where it belongs. Solicit feedback first, which means ask others to criticize your behavior. A go-to question helps because people with less power can prepare an honest answer. Do not treat the first polite reply as the whole answer.

Then give feedback to individuals. Praise counts. Specific praise tells someone what to repeat; vague approval just says you are pleased. Finally, encourage feedback between team members. Peers often see the issue first, and routing each hard fact through the boss slows the fix.
breakdown.fullRead:
Bob's failure is useful because it does not start with a loud mistake. At Juice Software, the soft pass buys a calm minute. Bob does not get the direct criticism. The person holding the fact feels kind, but Bob has less information than the job requires.

Trace the cost. First comes missing data. Bob keeps acting from the facts he has, while the needed fact sits elsewhere. If he guesses wrong, the miss can look like refusal instead of confusion.

Then comes lost time. Each easy exchange protects the speaker and charges Bob. The problem grows harder for everyone. By the time firing is near, the direct fact has to carry months of delay.

That is why the final talk can feel unfair even when the content is true. The hard fact arrives with the weight of a verdict. A useful warning has become late evidence. Who pays for the quiet?

Sandberg's case keeps the cure honest. Sheryl Sandberg managing Kim Scott at Google, in the account Scott published in 2017, is not proof that famous settings make directness right. It shows that trust changes how a hard observation lands. Without that base, the same hard line can sound like force.

This is where the limits live. Obnoxious Aggression means direct challenge without care; accurate criticism can still damage trust when the care signal is missing. Manipulative Insincerity means neither care nor direct challenge; the person protects image or advantage, and truth goes sideways. Silence is not neutral there.

The order is the guardrail. Solicit feedback before giving it. Ask the same plain question often enough that people can prepare a real answer. If the matter is urgent, do not use the order as an excuse to wait. Say the fact with care now, then ask what you should have done sooner.

After that, give feedback to individuals. Praise is not a soft extra. Specific praise tells someone what to repeat, so it belongs beside correction. Vague praise leaves the useful behavior hidden inside a warm feeling.

Then encourage feedback between team members. Peers often see the work first. If every concern waits for the boss, each fix waits too. The boss loses control over every hard sentence, but the people closest to the issue gain speed.

You can use the move with no title. Ask for criticism of your part before you correct someone else's. Name the fact while it can still help. When two people route an issue through you, ask what fact they should take to each other.

A kind delay is still a delay. The Bob story teaches that comfort has an owner: if you take it, the person who needed the fact pays.

examples.title: Standard Left Open
examples.scenario: Can Sheryl Sandberg name the hard standard before anyone knows how Kim Scott will use it? Yes. In the Google years, Sandberg is the senior manager, and she states the hard observation as guidance, not rank. Scott has not yet proved the result. The scene cuts there, with the fact finally available and the outcome still open.
examples.whatToDo: Ask whether the fact can still help. If it can, state the observation while it can affect the outcome, and keep the care signal plain.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask who would pay for silence. Copying the edge without the relationship risks humiliation, while waiting hides the fact altogether.

examples.title: Minute Already Spent
examples.scenario: Kim Scott is already taking in Sheryl Sandberg's hard observation; the demand is in the past. Sandberg, the manager Scott worked for in their Google years, has spent the awkward minute instead of buying comfort. The pause feels sharp. The move works because the relationship can bear direct guidance, and Scott gets the information while it can still matter.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what price is yours, then spend the awkward minute. Keep the fact tied to help, not rank, and stop when the useful point is clear.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask who gains from the minute. The receiver gets the fact before it goes stale, and the giver pays the cost instead of passing it forward.

examples.title: Ask Comes Due
examples.scenario: At the check-in, the earlier promise comes due: solicit feedback before giving it. The first reply is praise, and the manager running the Order of Operations nearly treats that as permission to give feedback to individuals. The miss is pulled back by another ask for criticism of their own behavior.
examples.whatToDo: Ask, "What did I do that made this harder?" Wait through the first polite answer. If the fact cannot wait, say it now and ask after.
examples.whyItMatters: Treat the order as credibility, not delay. Show you can receive criticism, but never let that rule hide a time-sensitive fact.

examples.title: Bob's Late Bill
examples.scenario: After the path toward firing has formed, Bob's manager at Juice Software can only trace the story backward. The first missed turn was delayed criticism. Bob did not get the clear fact early, so the real conversation became harder for everyone. The ending stays outside this scene; the visible bill is lost time.
examples.whatToDo: Skipping costs time first. Ask, "What fact is Bob still missing?" State that behavior before the only remaining talk is a final one.
examples.whyItMatters: Skipping costs fairness too. Late truth can sound like a verdict, because unclear feedback made the problem grow while everyone felt kind.

examples.title: Outside the Boss Path
examples.scenario: The lead first feels the drag outside the boss path: a peer sees the issue before the boss does. In the Order of Operations, after solicit feedback and give feedback to individuals, every hard fact still waits for one clearinghouse. After peers encourage feedback between team members, the fact reaches the person who can use it.
examples.whatToDo: Ask why this works: peers often see the task first. Have the people closest to the issue carry the fact to each other before it waits upward.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask what control costs: speed. When one boss clears every hard truth, the fix waits; direct peer guidance removes that delay.

examples.title: Praise With a Signal
examples.scenario: Is praise really guidance? Yes, if it tells the person what to repeat. In the Order of Operations, give feedback to individuals can still go wrong before peers encourage feedback between team members. Praise says only that the result was good. The note line stays blank. The miss is pulled back when praise names the observable behavior.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what should be repeated, then praise the observed behavior. Do not save specificity only for criticism; positive guidance needs a visible fact.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask what vague praise hides. It hides the useful move inside approval, so the person feels liked but cannot find the behavior again.

questions.prompt: During a volunteer shift, a coordinator keeps a weak habit comfortable until the helper has no chance to fix it. What caused the failure?
choices: The coordinator saved the hard fact for the most senior volunteer, so the helper heard status before help.
The coordinator made the correction sharp only at the end, so the helper mistook force for care.
The coordinator withheld a useful fact for comfort, so the helper missed the window to change.
questions.explanation: The failure is care without direct challenge. The senior-volunteer answer borrows authority, but the cause is simpler: the useful fact stayed hidden while change was possible.

questions.prompt: When a club chair hears only polite approval, which first move makes honest upward input more likely?
choices: Ask for criticism only after a visible failure, so helpers know the chair wants practical input, not status.
Let an assistant collect concerns first, so rank does not make the chair's request feel heavy.
Use the same plain question often, so helpers can prepare criticism before being put on the spot.
questions.explanation: The repeated question lowers the cost of speaking up. Asking only after a failure uses the right tool at the wrong trigger and makes candor episodic.

questions.prompt: A clinic supervisor admires Sandberg's directness and wants to copy it with a new aide. What should transfer?
choices: Start with the hard edge, so the aide learns high standards before personal comfort enters the talk.
Build enough trust for a hard observation to register as help, not humiliation.
Borrow the senior leader's wording, so the aide hears the correction as proven practice.
questions.explanation: The relationship is part of the mechanism. Borrowed wording is tempting, but it treats the case as style instead of trust carrying a hard point.

questions.prompt: After a lab project stalls, every concern waits for the sponsor though students saw the snag first. What should have happened earlier?
choices: Collect the concerns privately, then have the sponsor choose which student needs correction first, not peers.
Have the students carry the observable fact to each other, because peers often see the issue first.
Ask the sponsor to approve each sentence, so students can be direct without risking mismatch.
questions.explanation: The missed move is peer-to-peer correction. Private collection keeps the sponsor as clearinghouse, which is the delay this sequence removes.

questions.prompt: A startup founder delays a hard conversation because a developer seems fragile. Why is that default costly?
choices: Muddy criticism delays the real talk, so the issue grows harder for the developer and company.
Peer feedback arrives first, so the founder's later correction sounds like an unwanted second opinion from outside the real task.
Specific praise is missing, so the developer cannot tell which strong behavior should be repeated before hearing any concern.
questions.explanation: The Bob case prices delay. Peer input may matter elsewhere, but here the damage is that unclear feedback postpones the direct conversation.

questions.prompt: Before a department head asks staff to be more candid, which action belongs first?
choices: Give each person one clear correction, so the effort begins with standards everyone can see, not soft talk.
Send peers to correct one another, so honesty travels sideways without a boss in the middle.
Invite staff to criticize the head's own behavior, so later correction has proof of receptiveness.
questions.explanation: Get before give proves receptiveness. Starting with downward correction may be clear, but it skips the first proof that criticism can travel upward.

questions.prompt: In a condo vote, a member sees a flaw, stays quiet to avoid looking unprepared, then warns allies after. What damaged trust?
choices: She challenged without care, so the accurate point sounded harsh when the group was deciding.
She guarded her image, so feedback became political while the flaw stayed hidden.
She routed the point through the chair, so the right person heard it too early.
questions.explanation: The damage comes from evasion and side-channel warning. The harshness answer fits direct challenge without care, but this person avoided the direct challenge.

questions.prompt: During a lab handoff, a true criticism leaves the assistant shut down instead of clearer. What explains the miss?
choices: The lead challenged without a care signal, so accuracy damaged trust instead of helping.
The lead asked for criticism first, so the assistant heard the point as shared vulnerability.
The lead praised a repeatable behavior, so the assistant confused approval with correction.
questions.explanation: A true point can fail when care is absent. The upward-feedback answer names a valid step, but the scene shows a hard line that did not carry care.

questions.prompt: Your study partner improves one paragraph, and you want the move repeated later. Which response fits?
choices: Name the paragraph change itself, so your partner knows which behavior to repeat.
Keep praise general, so the warm part stays separate from any later criticism and feels easy to accept.
Ask a stronger writer to validate the praise, so the standard feels established.
questions.explanation: Specific praise is guidance because it marks repeatable behavior. General warmth is tempting, but it hides the very move you want to see again.

reviewCards.front: What comes before you give hard feedback?
reviewCards.back: Ask for criticism of your own behavior. Getting truth first proves that hard information can travel toward you, not only away from you.

reviewCards.front: Why can kind silence become unfair?
reviewCards.back: It can hide the fact a person needs while there is still time to use it. The comfort is yours now, but the lost chance is theirs later.

reviewCards.front: What does Bob at Juice Software warn you to price?
reviewCards.back: Price the delay. Bob, Juice Software, delayed criticism, and firing show how unclear feedback can turn a fixable gap into a late verdict.

reviewCards.front: What should you avoid copying from the Sandberg and Scott case?
reviewCards.back: Do not copy directness as mere style. Sheryl Sandberg managed Kim Scott at Google, and their story, told in 2017, shows that relationship trust helps the hard observation land.

reviewCards.front: What makes praise useful rather than merely warm?
reviewCards.back: Useful praise names the observable behavior to repeat. Vague approval may feel good, but it leaves the repeatable move hidden.

reviewCards.front: Why should peers sometimes speak before the boss path?
reviewCards.back: Peers often see the issue first. Routing every hard fact through one boss slows learning and makes people wait for permission to correct course.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Ask the First Question. Invite criticism of your own behavior before you give a hard line to someone else. Then give praise or correction as a specific fact while it can still help.

ifThenPlans.context: You are about to correct someone and the matter is not urgent.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I have time before I correct, then I will ask: "What did I do that made this harder?"

ifThenPlans.context: You need to give a time-sensitive correction.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the fact cannot wait, then I will say it with care now and ask afterward: "What should I have done sooner?"

ifThenPlans.context: Two peers route the same concern through you.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I become the clearinghouse, then I will ask: "What fact should you take directly to each other?"

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow noon, draft 1 exact ask you will use before a hard line: "What did I do that made your task harder?"
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every Friday for 15 minutes, observe where comfort delayed a fact, then note the first ask you will use the following week.

memorableLines.text: Guidance culture means praise and criticism move up, down, and across peers.
Every hidden fact sends the bill to the person you meant to spare.
Who pays for the quiet?

chapters.title: Understand What Motivates Each Person on Your Team
chapters.hook: Gloria's phone reminds her too late: she pushed a steady expert toward a path she did not want.
chapters.counterintuition: Fast growth is not the prize, and steady growth is not a warning sign. The useful question is what path fits the person now, because that answer can change.
chapters.tryThisNow: When a talent label lands in your notes, circle it for 60 seconds and replace it with one current signal.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat growth as a current route, not a rank: ask whether the person needs mastery, stretch, or a different level of support before you assign the role.

breakdown.fastRead:
Gloria's phone reminds her after the handoff slipped: she had called Patricia steady and stopped asking what Patricia wanted now. The cost was not drama. It was a skilled person aimed at the wrong lane.

Growth is a route, not a rank. Some seasons call for depth, mastery, and a stable role. Other seasons call for stretch and fast learning. You do not sort people once and manage from that file. You ask what kind of path the person is on now, then set support to match it. Circle the signal, not the status.
breakdown.deepRead:
Patricia can care deeply about the craft and still not want a bigger title. That is the part Gloria missed. She read low motion as low drive, so a stable expert became a problem to solve.

Growth Management names support for each person's growth trajectory, which means the path they need now. Rock Star Mode means gradual growth: mastery, depth, and stability. Superstar Mode means steep growth: fast learning and stretch. The names are not medals.

Gloria's first pass put Patricia in one box and Liliane in another. Patricia got pushed toward scope she did not seek. Liliane got kept comfortable after her role had gone flat. Both calls felt fair from far away. Up close, each balance was off: one needed room to master, the other needed a harder climb.

Are you helping the person in front of you, or the label you filed? Ask what the person is trying to learn, what kind of pace fits this season, and what support would make the next promise come back on a real date. You can do this without title power. Use it on your own projects: decide whether you are in a mastery stretch or a fast-learning stretch before you ask for more scope.

The role does not rank the person; the person changes the role.
breakdown.fullRead:
Gloria's harder case was not Patricia, the steady expert. It was the part of Gloria that wanted a neat talent map. A map feels clean. People do not stay clean for long. A new child, a hard year, a new skill, or a dull role can shift the pace a person wants. You lose the signal when you turn one season into a trait.

Rock Star Mode is easy to insult by accident. If you hear steady and translate it as stuck, you will push mastery out of the role that most needs it. Some roles run on stored judgment. They need the person who has seen many edge cases and still wants to get better at the craft. Underestimating someone who is not seeking promotion is one of the framework's named risks. Ambition can point toward craft, not hierarchy.

Superstar Mode has its own trap. Restlessness is not an automatic claim on a bigger title. Stretch has to fit the work, the person's readiness, and the group around them. Give a restless person scope with no fit and you may create churn or failure. Hold a steep-growth person too close and you may clip the wings that made them valuable. The climb does not prove the person; the fit proves the climb.

A balanced team needs both paths. Continuity and change solve different problems. If everyone is racing toward the next hill, no one may stay long enough to hold the old learning. If everyone is settled, the group may miss the new chance. Balance is not a quota. It is a live ledger: who is learning fast, who is deepening craft, and which promise is drifting because the wrong support is attached.

Support is where the idea becomes visible. Micromanagement means too much control; absentee management means too little help. The same habit can harm in opposite ways. Gloria's daily check-ins helped Liliane when the task was new, then began to choke her once she needed space. Patricia liked autonomy, but Gloria's hands-off style became absence when Patricia needed public respect for mastery. Same habit, different cost.

You can use the lens on yourself. When you ask for a new role, do not hide behind ready for more. Name what kind of more you mean. More depth? More pace? More help? More space? If you want stability for a season, say what craft you are building there. If you want stretch, say what result will make it worth the risk. That answer is more useful than a badge.

Do not use this move when the issue is clear harm, a missed standard, or a skill gap that must be fixed now. Fix the standard first. Growth mode does not excuse bad work, and stretch should not become a prize for restlessness. The cost of the move is time: you have to keep asking, because the promise comes back on a date, or it drifts.

examples.title: Gloria Reopens the Label
examples.scenario: The phone reminder glowed after the transfer failed. Director Gloria traced the miss backward: she had used Growth Management as a form with a fixed box, not as a fresh read of growth trajectory and role fit. Patricia accepted the new scope, then gave it back. The move still worked when Gloria paid the cost: she admitted the label had outrun the person.
examples.whatToDo: Trace the promise back to the label you used. Circle the current signal, ask what role fit changed, and replace the fixed box with one support choice.
examples.whyItMatters: Treat the cost as useful. A failed scope call tells you where growth trajectory moved; ignoring it makes the old label the real boss.

examples.title: Patricia Holds the Craft
examples.scenario: Outside the staffing room, the client first felt the effect: the handoff lost the one person who knew the old edge cases. Operations lead Patricia had been tagged as low ambition because she wanted mastery, the gradual growth named in Rock Star Mode. Gloria almost filled the role with a fast climber, then stopped barely in time and kept Patricia close to the craft.
examples.whatToDo: Price the miss before you fill the role. Name what mastery protects, then ask Patricia whether gradual growth or new scope fits the season.
examples.whyItMatters: Skipping this drains stored judgment. Rock Star Mode is not a consolation label; it names value that can hold a fragile role steady.

examples.title: Genevieve Asks Too Late
examples.scenario: A cold mug sat beside engineer Genevieve while the quiet problem kept growing. Gloria gave her the same light touch that worked for Patricia, but Genevieve was in Superstar Mode and wanted steep growth with stretch challenges. Gloria finally added scope. It half-worked: the learning returned, but the old absence had taught Genevieve not to ask early.
examples.whatToDo: Rebalance the support before the person stops asking. Gloria adds a harder task, sets one follow-up, and keeps contact brief.
examples.whyItMatters: Protect learning energy, then adjust the move. Stretch helps Superstar Mode, but delayed support can leave a residue that one new task cannot clear.

examples.title: Liliane Separates Stretch
examples.scenario: Product lead Liliane stated the demand plainly: she wanted a bigger title because the role felt too small. Gloria could have treated Superstar Mode and its steep growth as an entitlement. Instead she separated stretch from status, tested fit and readiness, and gave Liliane a harder problem without the title. It worked, but the cost was a tense no before the better yes.
examples.whatToDo: Ask the hard question: what stretch serves the work now? Gloria gives scope tied to fit, readiness, and context, not a title by default.
examples.whyItMatters: Answer the fear first: no title is not no growth. Fit protects Liliane from churn and protects the work from a challenge too large or too soon.

examples.title: Gloria Splits Support
examples.scenario: The car key clicked in the parked car as project lead Gloria changed course mid-call. The demand had already passed: Genevieve wanted space, Patricia wanted visible backing. One default, more oversight for both, had seemed fair until Growth Management brought role fit back into view. Had she not stopped, one habit would have over-controlled one person and abandoned the other.
examples.whatToDo: Split the default before it hardens. Give Genevieve space, give Patricia visible backing, and stop calling one habit fair for both.
examples.whyItMatters: Fit changes support. One style can over-control one person and abandon another, so equal attention can still be unfair when the paths differ.

questions.prompt: After Liliane's fast-learning role became routine, she stopped taking harder tasks and asked to leave. Which earlier miss best explains the failure?
choices: The lead treated the role title as enough proof that Liliane still had useful scope, even after the learning curve had already flattened.
The lead failed to add real stretch for someone in a steep-growth season, so the stable role began to waste her learning drive.
The lead offered every person the same stretch at the same time, turning a single growth need into a broad staffing change.
questions.explanation: The miss is underuse of steep growth. The role-title answer is tempting, but a title is weak proof once the learning curve has gone flat.

questions.prompt: When Genevieve keeps asking for harder scope and her lead delays because the current setup is easier to run, what is actually going wrong?
choices: Her lead is asking for stretch too early, before Genevieve has shown any sign that the present role is too small.
Her lead is keeping a steep-growth person comfortable for ease, which can turn learning energy into frustration.
Her lead is solving the wrong person's problem by asking Patricia to absorb the same stretch Genevieve wants, even though Patricia seeks mastery.
questions.explanation: The risk is clipped stretch. Patricia is a plausible distraction, but this symptom sits with Genevieve's delayed scope, not Patricia's mastery path.

questions.prompt: A growth call already failed after the staffing lead sorted everyone into high and low potential at the start of the quarter. Which earlier step caused the miss?
choices: The lead waited too long to publish the labels, so people could not tell where they stood before assignments changed.
The lead used fit only for Patricia's role, so the rest of the group got the same fixed category without a current read.
The lead treated a moving growth path as a permanent talent rank instead of reading the person's current signal.
questions.explanation: Growth Management asks for a fresh read. The publish-the-labels option only makes the fixed-rank error clearer and earlier.

questions.prompt: Liliane has become restless and asks for a bigger title by Friday. What should the staffing lead do before granting it?
choices: Test whether stretch fits the work, Liliane's readiness, and the group context before deciding whether title change belongs.
Give the title now because restlessness proves steep growth and steep growth should move upward fast, even without fit evidence.
Delay all stretch until the next cycle, because bigger scope is risky whenever a person asks for it directly.
questions.explanation: Superstar Mode is not an entitlement. The always-upward choice borrows the right signal, restlessness, then treats it as settled proof.

questions.prompt: In a staffing call, Patricia says she does not want promotion, but the fragile role depends on her stored judgment. Which diagnosis best fits the evidence?
choices: Patricia has become complacent, so the lead should move the role to a faster climber before mastery slows change.
Patricia may be in a gradual-growth mode where mastery and stability are central to strong performance.
Patricia should receive the same stretch as Liliane, because all ambition has to move toward more scope.
questions.explanation: Rock Star Mode treats mastery as value. The complacency answer fails by mistaking gradual growth for low care.

questions.prompt: The staffing lead marks Patricia as steady forever after one good mastery season. What happens downstream if that choice guides later roles?
choices: Patricia's later change in ambition gets missed, because a mode that should describe a season has become identity.
Patricia receives too much stretch at once, because the lead is treating all steady experts as secret fast climbers.
Patricia's craft gets valued more clearly, because permanent labels make support simpler and easier to explain.
questions.explanation: A mode is seasonal. The simpler-support choice sounds efficient, yet it is exactly how a useful label hardens into identity.

questions.prompt: Genevieve feels smothered by daily oversight while Patricia feels left alone when her craft needs visible backing. Which move fits?
choices: Change the support level by person, giving Genevieve more space and Patricia more backing instead of using one default.
Keep the same style for both people, because equal treatment proves the lead is not playing favorites with growth paths, even when needs diverge.
Switch both people to full autonomy, because micromanagement is the only real trajectory failure in the pair.
questions.explanation: The same habit can over-control one person and abandon another. Full autonomy fixes only half the pattern and leaves Patricia exposed.

questions.prompt: Suppose every role is built around fast climbers while steady experts get moved out of the core path. What is the likely cost?
choices: The group gains more reliable depth, because fast climbers naturally preserve the old craft while taking on new scope.
The balance improves, because gradual growth is mainly useful when a role has already become less important.
The group loses continuity and stored expertise, because change and stability solve different problems.
questions.explanation: Balance needs both modes. The reliable-depth answer reverses the mechanism by asking fast climbers to supply the stability just removed.

questions.prompt: During a failed staffing choice, Patricia was assumed to care less because she did not seek promotion. Which earlier correction was missing?
choices: The lead should have pushed Patricia toward hierarchy sooner, because craft focus becomes ambition only after promotion is offered.
The lead should have delayed all role talk until Patricia asked for it, because stable contributors do not need active support.
The lead should have asked how Patricia's ambition showed up in craft and stability instead of equating care with promotion hunger.
questions.explanation: Ambition can aim at craft. The delay-all-talk option spots stability but wrongly turns it into neglect.

reviewCards.front: What is Growth Management trying to replace?
reviewCards.back: It replaces fixed talent labels with a fresh read of current growth trajectory and role fit. The person may need mastery, stretch, more support, or less control this season.

reviewCards.front: How does Rock Star Mode differ from complacency?
reviewCards.back: Rock Star Mode names gradual growth and mastery. The person may care deeply about craft, stability, and stored judgment without wanting a bigger title right now.

reviewCards.front: What does Superstar Mode ask you to watch for?
reviewCards.back: Superstar Mode points to steep growth, rapid learning, and need for stretch challenges. If the role stays flat too long, learning energy can become frustration.

reviewCards.front: Why can a non-promotion path still show ambition?
reviewCards.back: Ambition can aim at craft instead of hierarchy. A person may choose stability and still care deeply about mastery, reliability, and the quality of the work.

reviewCards.front: When does stretch become unsafe?
reviewCards.back: Stretch becomes unsafe when it ignores fit, readiness, or group context. Restlessness is a signal to inspect, not a claim that a bigger title is owed.

reviewCards.front: How can one support habit fail two people?
reviewCards.back: A habit can over-control one person and abandon another. The level of help has to fit the person's current path, not your favorite style.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Circle the Current Signal. Use one current sign of pace or support before you name someone's path. A label can help only after you have asked whether the person needs mastery, stretch, more help, or more space.

ifThenPlans.context: Circle a fixed label.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you write steady, high potential, or a similar label, then replace it with one recent sign before you act.

ifThenPlans.context: Count the restless ask.
ifThenPlans.plan: If someone asks for more scope, then test fit, readiness, and group cost before you offer a title.

ifThenPlans.context: Mark the support mismatch.
ifThenPlans.plan: If one habit is choking one person and leaving another alone, then change the level of help for each.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During your next morning calendar scan, circle 1 fixed label you have put on a person or project and spend 5 minutes replacing it with one current need.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday, measure one number: how many times you named a current need before assigning scope, stability, help, or space. Try to raise it by 1.

memorableLines.text: Are you helping the person in front of you, or the label you filed?
Circle the signal, not the status.
The climb does not prove the person; the fit proves the climb.

chapters.title: Drive Results Collaboratively
chapters.hook: The fastest decision can be the slowest collaboration move when the miss lands downstream.
chapters.counterintuition: Collaboration fails when you treat it like one good habit. The GSD Wheel splits it into seven jobs, and the skipped job names the failure to fix.
chapters.tryThisNow: Schedule 10 minutes before your next shared call: name the step most likely to be skipped, then write who owes whom what by when.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use the GSD Wheel as a fault finder. Listen for missing facts, clarify rough ideas, debate the work, decide near facts, persuade, execute, and learn.

breakdown.fastRead: The fastest decision can slow the whole effort. Nathan hears the demand on a lunch break: pick the customer fix now, before the queue backs up. He takes the first clear answer, skips the quiet risk, and the customer gets the wrong step. The GSD Wheel is a seven-step path for shared results: Listen, Clarify, Debate, Decide, Persuade, Execute, and Learn. Each step does a different job. Skip Listen, and facts never enter. Skip Clarify, and a rough idea gets hit before it is clear. Without Persuade, the people asked to act inherit a choice they do not trust.
breakdown.deepRead:
The GSD Wheel, the Get Stuff Done cycle, separates seven jobs that often get mashed into one call. It moves through Listen, then Clarify, then Debate, then Decide, then Persuade, then Execute, then Learn. That matters because each skipped job fails in its own way. Listen gives quieter people a way in before the first voice frames the facts. Clarify lets a rough thought become clear enough to face pressure. Debate tests the idea. Decide keeps the call close to facts.

Use the wheel with judgment. If a small task already has a clear answer, do not force all seven steps. If more talk would only add collaboration tax, protect Execute and let people do the task. The cost is real: time, strain, and slower action. This is not a plea for more talk. It is the check that fires before the miss.

Steve Jobs's rock tumbler metaphor, the source image for Debate, makes the hard part visible. Ordinary rocks become smooth because they rub against each other. Ideas can improve the same way, but only when the pressure stays on the idea and off the person. Debate is the rock tumbler, not the rock fight.

One listening self-test asks whether managers are quiet listeners or loud listeners. That is not a style quiz. It asks who your default leaves out. A loud listener may crowd the first frame. A quiet listener may let silence hide risk. Either way, Listen needs a method.

The shorthand Aristotle three elements means emotion, credibility, and logic, and it gives the Persuade step a plain job. Why sell a call after it is made? Because some people must act on a choice they did not help form. They need the feeling named, the source trusted, and the reason clear. Skip Persuade, and the cost shows up as slow execution.
breakdown.fullRead:
You do not need a title to use the wheel. If Nathan owes Reid an answer, Nathan can still run the first two jobs. He asks what Reid has seen, then restates the rough idea until Reid says it is right. No title needed.

Listen is not waiting while the loudest person talks first. It is a design for getting facts into the open before the first frame hardens. The quiet-listener or loud-listener self-test belongs here. Your style has a process cost. If the same people always speak, you are not hearing the full field.

Clarify is the pause before the fight. A rough idea is easy to crush because the first version is often clumsy. Make it clear enough to deserve a fair test. Ask what the idea would change, who would feel it, and what problem it is trying to solve. Then Debate has something real to hit.

Debate and Decide are close, but they are not the same job. Debate lets strong views meet under pressure while ego stays out. Decide ends the rub and moves the call toward the facts. When Reid has rank and Camden has the constraint, the better call may sit closer to Camden. The boss who grabs every choice can separate the answer from the best information.

Persuade is not a victory lap. It is the handoff to people who were not in the earlier argument. Noemie cannot ask for action and skip the reason. She has to carry the feeling, the trusted source, and the reason. People need to know what concern was heard, why the source can be trusted, and how the choice fits the facts.

Execute protects time from the drag of coordination. This is where collaboration can betray itself. One more call can look helpful while it steals the space needed to finish. When the missing step is Execute, the kind move is often to remove noise, not add a larger circle.

Learn is the step pride wants to skip. After people spend effort on a choice, the old choice starts to feel like proof of judgment. But the result gets a vote. If the result shows a miss, the wheel starts again. The loop that closes is not the one that ends with action. It is the one that lets evidence speak.

So use the GSD Wheel as a fault finder. Where did the loss begin? If people were surprised by the task, look at Persuade. If the argument kept circling, look at Clarify. If rank overran facts, look at Decide. If the same miss returned, look at Learn. The fastest path is not the shortest path. It is the path that does not skip the job that would have caught the failure.

examples.title: Nathan Lets the First Answer Win
examples.scenario: Support lead Nathan states the demand during a lunch break: choose the customer fix now so the queue can move. He treats the first clear answer as enough and skips a listening pass in the GSD Wheel. A junior sees the risk but never gets asked. The customer is not in that exchange; she only feels the miss when the fix fails and she has to come back.
examples.whatToDo: When the first answer sounds clean, listening works because it captures facts before debate hardens. Nathan asks each quiet person for one risk before Clarify.
examples.whyItMatters: When the customer must live with the answer, the quiet risk is not a courtesy. It is the fact that keeps a fast choice from becoming rework.

examples.title: Camden Adds Contact Before Friction
examples.scenario: Camden is dragging a blue calendar block across an already packed afternoon. The demand to finish the spec has passed. He wants another status call because execution stalled, but the skipped step sits earlier: nobody let the two designs collide. Steve Jobs's rock tumbler metaphor says Debate uses friction on the idea, not ego. Camden sends the invite. The result is still unknown.
examples.whatToDo: When execution stalls, ask what failed before the stall. If Debate was skipped, schedule one focused clash over the idea before adding coordination.
examples.whyItMatters: When peace was bought by avoiding friction, more contact will not strengthen the choice. The rock tumbler belongs before the invite spreads.

examples.title: Noemie Earns the Handoff
examples.scenario: At the project check-in in the group chat, project lead Noemie answers for the choice she promised to carry. Earlier, a small group changed the handoff, but the people who must carry it did not hear the reasoning. One person says the old path was safer. Noemie slows down and uses the Persuade step through Aristotle three elements: emotion, credibility, and logic. The handoff moves after that.
examples.whatToDo: When people missed the argument, persuade before assigning. Name the feeling, earn trust, give the reason, then ask for action.
examples.whyItMatters: Once the choice reaches late actors, a bare task asks for faith they may not owe. Persuasion gives them the reason before execution starts.

examples.title: Reid Finds the Missing Verb
examples.scenario: After the customer fix is over, project partner Reid studies one fact: six verbs were logged, but the GSD Wheel has seven. A red mark sits beside the blank Learn line. The group is ready to repeat the old fix because defending it looks steady. Reid stops the repeat, asks what the result proves, and changes the next handoff before the same miss reaches another customer.
examples.whatToDo: After results arrive, schedule Learn before defending the old choice. Name the evidence, change one action, and stop the repeat before it leaves.
examples.whyItMatters: After consistency starts to sound noble, treat it as cost. Let the result reopen the wheel, or the old miss ships twice.

questions.prompt: After the result disappoints, Camden wants to defend the old plan so he looks steady. What happens downstream if he treats that defense as leadership?
choices: He asks for one lesson, but treats it as a note for later while keeping the same choice in place.
He lets consistency outrank evidence, so the wheel cannot restart around what the result just proved.
He treats the miss as permission to reopen every settled point, even the parts the result did not touch.
questions.explanation: Learn exists so results can restart the wheel. The first choice sounds reflective, but it still protects the old call from the evidence.

questions.prompt: During a product dispute, Reid wants each side to speak once and then choose without a clash. Which principle does that plan break?
choices: Save disagreement until execution stalls, because friction is useful only after a chosen idea starts to fail.
Collect both views, then stop as soon as the points conflict so the exchange stays easy to absorb.
Use focused friction before the call, with the two designs taking pressure instead of the people arguing.
questions.explanation: Debate tests the idea before Decide. Letting each side speak once is only a half-step; it avoids the friction that would expose weak edges.

questions.prompt: Noemie's sessions keep producing ideas from the same voices while quieter people hold back useful risks. What best explains why her listening method needs repair?
choices: Her own quiet-or-loud default is shaping who gets heard, so she needs a method that offsets that bias.
Her rough-idea step is weak, so she should clarify every proposal after debate has already started and the first frame is set.
Her rank is too hidden, so she should take the decision early before new voices change the frame and slow the exchange.
questions.explanation: The quiet-or-loud prompt is about style shaping participation. The clarify answer treats the wrong step; the loss starts before debate.

questions.prompt: Execution has stalled, and Nathan proposes another status call. What should come first if coordination load is the bottleneck?
choices: Add a wider call so every person can restate progress before anyone returns to the task that is already starved for time.
Reopen the original debate, including parts already settled by facts close to the task and ready for action.
Protect execution space by removing coordination load before adding another contact point.
questions.explanation: Execute reduces collaboration tax. A wider status call may look responsive, but it adds the load that is already slowing the task.

questions.prompt: During a lunch-break support fix, Camden lets the first confident speaker frame the answer before asking others in. What failure is most likely?
choices: Useful facts vanish before debate begins, especially from people who needed a clearer way into the exchange.
The final call moves too close to the facts, making formal authority less visible than it should be to others.
The execution block becomes too protected, leaving people with too little contact after the choice.
questions.explanation: Listen is meant to surface facts before the first frame hardens. The authority concern belongs to Decide, not to this early loss.

questions.prompt: A project has many calls but cannot name whether it is stuck in listening, debate, decision, or execution. Why does the GSD Wheel help?
choices: It treats collaboration as one broad habit, so the group can improve tone before naming a narrower failure or changing any step.
It separates the effort into seven jobs, so the skipped step points to the bottleneck instead of a vague need for more talk.
It moves every call to the most senior person, so decisions happen faster when tension rises.
questions.explanation: The seven verbs diagnose different stalls. The tone answer feels useful, but it keeps the actual bottleneck unnamed.

questions.prompt: After a small group decides, Noemie sends only the task to people who must carry it out and skips the reasons. Which flaw does that reveal?
choices: She reopened debate too late, asking late actors to argue a choice after the facts had already settled.
She failed to transfer reason, trust, and felt stakes to people who were not part of the earlier debate.
She listened too broadly, letting people outside the task change a decision they were only asked to execute.
questions.explanation: Persuade carries understanding to people outside the earlier path. Reopening debate is a different miss; this handoff is too bare.

questions.prompt: Reid has the title, but Camden is closest to the constraint. Which move fits Decide best?
choices: Move the call toward Camden's facts, so the choice stays near the information that can reveal the constraint.
Ask Camden for input, then have Reid decide anyway so authority remains visible after the facts are gathered.
Hand every future decision to Camden because closeness to one constraint should override role and scope.
questions.explanation: Decide pushes the call toward the facts. Asking Camden for input but defaulting to rank still separates the choice from the best information.

questions.prompt: In a support handoff, a rough fix appears, and Nathan starts debating it before anyone can restate it clearly. What is the likely failure?
choices: People will spend persuasion effort too early, giving late actors reasons before a real choice exists.
People will protect execution time too soon, leaving too little contact for a task that is already settled.
People may reject a distorted version of the idea because it was tested before it was made clear.
questions.explanation: Clarify protects rough ideas before testing. The persuasion answer jumps ahead; this failure happens before a real choice exists.

reviewCards.front: What problem does the GSD Wheel solve?
reviewCards.back: It stops you from treating collaboration as one vague habit. The seven steps name different jobs, so a skipped step points to a specific failure.

reviewCards.front: Why does Listen need a method?
reviewCards.back: The best idea may not come from the first or loudest person. A listening method gives quieter people a way in before debate hardens around the first frame.

reviewCards.front: What does Clarify protect?
reviewCards.back: It protects rough ideas from being rejected too soon. A clumsy first version may hold value, but it needs clear form before debate can test it fairly.

reviewCards.front: When does debate help rather than harm?
reviewCards.back: Debate helps when friction stays on the idea and off the person. The rock tumbler image matters because pressure can make the idea smoother without making anyone the enemy.

reviewCards.front: Why does Persuade need more than a task?
reviewCards.back: People who missed the earlier debate need understanding before action. Aristotle's triad names what must travel: emotion, credibility, and logic.

reviewCards.front: What does Learn do after results arrive?
reviewCards.back: Learn restarts the wheel. It asks what the result now proves, so loyalty to the old choice does not block correction.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Schedule the Missing Step. Before a shared effort moves, name the step most likely to be skipped and put time around that one step. Keep it small: a listening pass, a clarification pass, a focused debate, a fact-near decision, a persuasion handoff, protected execution space, or a learning pass after results.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe who speaks first in a shared call, then note whose facts have not been invited.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the first voice is carrying the frame, then schedule a 10-minute listening pass before debate starts.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe a rough idea getting criticized, then note whether anyone can state it clearly.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the idea is still fuzzy, then schedule a 10-minute clarification pass before testing it.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe a choice reaching people late, then note which reason they never heard.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the people doing the task missed the argument, then schedule a 15-minute persuasion handoff before asking for action.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before your next recurring status call, schedule 15 minutes for the missing step you can name now. Put the verb in the invite title and include only the people needed for that verb.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For the coming week, use this trigger: if a shared effort stalls, then schedule the missing step within 24 hours and write one sentence about what changed.

memorableLines.text: The fastest decision can slow the whole effort.
Debate is the rock tumbler, not the rock fight.
Skip Persuade, and the cost shows up as slow execution.

chapters.title: Relationships
chapters.hook: 20 languages can carry the training; one trust miss can make Theodore's candor ring hollow.
chapters.counterintuition: Trust is not the soft part before the tools. It is the load-bearing routine that lets later candor land without sounding like power in a nicer coat.
chapters.tryThisNow: Read aloud one request for candor for 5 minutes. Watch whether it asks you to receive first, then write down the first power signal you hear.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Relationships are not warm-up talk. They are trust routines that make later candor bearable: stay centered, notice strain, build visible proof, and get before you give.

breakdown.fastRead:
20 languages can carry a method across offices, but Theodore still loses the moment if Lucy hears advice before she sees him receive truth. Radical Candor LLC is described as a global executive education company; its page says the work has been translated into 20 languages. That scale matters because the first tool cannot depend on one office mood.

Relationships opens Part 2, the tools and techniques section. It starts with trust routines: repeatable acts that show power is not the only force in the link. The order matters. Stay centered. Notice when strain keeps you from showing up well. Ask what direct reports can observe when you build trust. Then receive before you advise: seek criticism before handing it out. If Theodore skips that order, every later script charges trust he has not paid into.
breakdown.deepRead:
Receiving first lowers the price of honesty. When a boss asks for hard truth before giving it, the other person sees that candor is not a one-way toll. Every advice-first habit charges trust before anyone has a chance to earn it.

Project lead Theodore wants to help analyst Lucy, and his first draft starts with advice. Then the Relationships prompts slow him down. They ask what keeps him centered, when strain had made him reactive, and which visible acts let direct reports trust him. Those are not private diary questions. They name the places where strain leaks into behavior.

Aurelie, a department head, feels the same cost. She can ask for candor only after she has shown how she handles strain. If she snaps, then asks for openness, she has made the hard truth more expensive. Ask first, then advise.

Order of Operations is the official sequence across Chapters 5-6: solicit feedback, give feedback to individuals, then encourage it among peers. Relationships uses the first move as relationship work. Get before you give means Theodore asks what Lucy sees in him before he tells her what he sees in her.

Who pays when the first trust signal appears only after the fight? Lucy does. She has to risk the truth while Theodore keeps the safer role. Price the trust signal before you ask for candor. If the price all lands on the person with less power, the routine has not begun.
breakdown.fullRead:
Lisa's training note gives the scale without making scale the lesson. That page also notes a 20-language reach. The useful point is not size. It is that a relationship practice has to travel as behavior, not as a local custom. That is why Lisa keeps the repeated ask and cuts the local custom before it hardens.

The chronology is spare. Part 2 begins with Relationships. That unit asks you to name activities that keep you centered. It asks when you could not bring your best self to work. It asks how trust is built with direct reports. Then the order across Chapters 5-6 begins with soliciting feedback. The pressure rises only after that.

That order reverses the move many people make under stress. You feel a miss, so you reach for a script, a sharper line, or a formal tool. But relationship work comes before Guidance, Team, and Results because those later tools carry more heat. Crisis is a poor time to build the first proof of trust.

What has Theodore done that makes hard truth less costly for Lucy? If the answer is nothing, his next sentence should not be advice. It should be a request he can bear to hear answered. Small counts here. A steady pause before reply. A real question about his conduct. A visible change when the answer hurts.

The limit matters. If Lucy needs a clear standard now, Theodore cannot hide inside endless listening. Trust routines are not delay tactics. They break when the person with power keeps asking for feelings but never makes a hard call. In that case, the cost has merely moved, and Lucy still pays it.

You can use the move without a title. Before you correct a partner, a volunteer, or a classmate, ask whether you have made truth safe in both directions. If you have not, receive first. If you already asked and did nothing with the answer, do not ask again as theater. Change one visible behavior.

That is why the training context belongs here. A company can teach a routine; it cannot teach chemistry on command. Translation into 20 languages points to the portable piece: stay centered, invite criticism upward, and build trust through repeated proof. Not charm. Not rank. Proof.

Theodore does not need a grand confession. He needs to lower the cost of Lucy's next true sentence. He can name the strain that makes him defensive, ask where it shows up, and make one change she can see. Receiving first is not a slogan here. It is the first receipt.

examples.title: The Ask Comes Late
examples.scenario: After the Friday handoff on the support floor, project lead Theodore traced the miss after his direct report stopped adding facts. He had ignored the Order of Operations: solicit feedback, then give it. A cold mug still sat beside him from the earlier exchange. He called back and used get before give, asking what he made harder to say. The answer had not arrived when the call ended.
examples.whatToDo: Theodore asks for one hard truth before any advice.
examples.whyItMatters: Theodore moves power down first.

examples.title: The Delay Lands
examples.scenario: During a Monday staffing call in operations, department head Aurelie first made the effect visible when she delayed a sharp reply. Before the prompt, strain became speed, and the speed sounded like blame. After it, Aurelie named the activity that helped her stay centered and said build trust with direct reports had to include her own pause. "I wanted to react," Aurelie said. "I chose to come back steadier." A hard fact came back.
examples.whatToDo: Aurelie gives you the command: name the act that steadies you before you ask another person for candor.
examples.whyItMatters: Aurelie makes the other person pay less when she carries her own strain first.

examples.title: The Custom Almost Travels
examples.scenario: In facilitator prep for a training cohort, Lisa rewrites the first exercise before the slides lock. The draft treats Radical Candor LLC, a global executive education company, as if relationships were private chemistry from one office culture. The official page says the work has been translated into 20 languages, so she replaces the local ritual with one repeatable ask: what have you done that makes truth safer to give you?
examples.whatToDo: Lisa keeps the 20-language clue in view: preserve the behavior that can be practiced twice, not the office custom that happened to carry it once.
examples.whyItMatters: The redesign makes the routine teachable. Relationship trust has to travel as an observable act, because chemistry cannot scale on command.

examples.title: The Standard Is Earned
examples.scenario: During a project-group trust check, Lucy tests Theodore's claim against what direct reports can actually observe. His intent sounds clear to him because the title is his; it does not lower the risk for her. The standard is build trust through evidence, not assumption. Until Theodore names a practice she can see twice, the claim remains only a promise from the person with more power.
examples.whatToDo: Make trust observable. Name the practice another person can see, then repeat it before asking them to risk a sharper truth.
examples.whyItMatters: Theodore cannot borrow trust from his title. Repeated evidence is the move that lowers the risk for the direct report.

examples.title: The Advice Gets Deleted
examples.scenario: Why is Theodore deleting the advice he already wrote? Because the Order of Operations starts when he solicits feedback, and get before give means the first move is to receive. He is cutting the first line now. The cursor blinks at the start of his note. He changes "Here is what you should do" to "What am I missing in how I handle this?" A hard truth comes back. He waits to advise until he has heard it.
examples.whatToDo: Theodore answers the reader's worry: yes, the cost is waiting; ask upward before giving counsel.
examples.whyItMatters: The other person can test whether candor is reciprocal. The delay buys trust that a fast answer would spend.

examples.title: The Strain Gets Named
examples.scenario: At the check-in itself, Aurelie answered for the commitment she had made. She had promised to stay centered by naming the moment when she could not bring her best self to work. The first answer blamed pressure. The miss was close. Then she named the real pattern: when strained, she answered too fast. Lisa asked for the safeguard before direct reports felt the cost.
examples.whatToDo: Aurelie names one failure point before blame.
examples.whyItMatters: Lisa gets a safeguard, not a mood report.

questions.prompt: Several actions look useful at the start of a tools section when a new lead wants better candor after a guarded exchange. Which comes first, and why?
choices: Start by earning trust through a repeatable relationship habit, because later feedback can only carry what that habit has made credible.
Start by selecting a stronger script for the difficult talk, because cleaner wording can make missing trust less visible when strain rises.
Start by asking the most senior person which tactic to use, because rank can stand in for relationship proof when the habit is weak.
questions.explanation: The first tool is trust-building behavior. The script answer tempts because wording matters, but scripts still fail when trust is absent.
