questions.prompt: A neighborhood volunteer group wants to borrow this move after members say the tone depends on who shows up. What maps best from the training context?
choices: Let the warmest member set the tone for every hard exchange, because relationship skill depends mainly on personal chemistry.
Turn trust into a repeatable habit the group can practice, because the training context treats relationships as teachable behavior.
Ask a respected outside brand to settle the standard for the group, because borrowed standing can replace local trust.
questions.explanation: The training context points to routines that can be taught. Warm chemistry is close enough to sound kind, but this move rejects chemistry as the core tool.

questions.prompt: The rollout already failed: candor appeared only after conflict got hot, and the first trust signal came under pressure. What earlier step caused the miss?
choices: They used too few talk tracks, so pressure rose because the later words were not carefully chosen for the hardest exchange.
They chose the wrong later tool, even though a trust base had already been built before pressure rose and stayed visible.
They waited for a performance problem before building the first trust signal, so conflict arrived before capacity.
questions.explanation: The cause is late trust-building. The talk-track answer is plausible, but it treats wording as the gap when timing caused the failure.

questions.prompt: Before a supervisor asks a direct report to accept hard input after weeks of guarded answers, which priority fits the order taught here?
choices: Give the direct report the hard input first, because seeing the standard early will make later upward candor easier for both sides.
Set peers up to exchange criticism first, because sideways candor removes the pressure from the supervisor's role before she receives any.
Ask what the supervisor needs to hear about her own behavior, because receiving first makes candor reciprocal.
questions.explanation: The sequence begins with soliciting feedback. Peer exchange is a real later move, but using it first skips the power-lowering act.

questions.prompt: A supervisor keeps giving careful advice after every update, yet the sharp fact stays hidden and the relationship feels polite but thin. What is actually wrong?
choices: He offers counsel before proving he can hear hard truth, so the exchange still runs one way.
He asks for too much candor from below, so he should return to advice until others trust his expertise.
He lacks a formal title for the exchange, so a role label should create the permission his behavior has not earned.
questions.explanation: Get before give means he must receive first. Waiting to ask for candor sounds safer, but it keeps power moving one way.

questions.prompt: At a school club, an older student wants younger members to speak honestly after a tense practice. What maps from this move?
choices: Give repeated, visible proof that honesty is safe, because power makes trust something the older student must earn.
Assume the younger members trust the older student by default, because shared club membership creates enough safety.
Aim the trust routine at the club handbook, because the written rule can carry what the older student has not shown.
questions.explanation: The power gap makes evidence necessary. The handbook answer borrows the right idea of proof but aims it at a document instead of behavior.

questions.prompt: A supervisor snaps twice, then asks for candor and gets guarded answers from people with less power. Which repair starts closest to the cause?
choices: Treat composure as a private wellness matter and keep it separate from how others decide whether to trust her.
Name one activity that keeps her centered before the next hard exchange, because her state affects the relationship.
Ask the direct report to be more resilient during tense exchanges, because that person can absorb strain while trust develops.
questions.explanation: Centering is relationship protection, not private decoration. Asking the other person to absorb strain moves the cost downward.

questions.prompt: A volunteer adapts the routine for a club with a different culture. What should she preserve?
choices: Copy the original office custom closely, because the known scene has already carried the method elsewhere.
Let the local status order decide who may speak first, because translation means each culture supplies the trust signal.
Keep the behavior small and portable, because the useful piece is repeated trust behavior rather than one office style.
questions.explanation: The 20-language fact points to portable behavior. Copying the office custom feels faithful, but it mistakes one setting for the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A supervisor's last attempt failed after strain leaked into her answer and the other person stopped being candid. Which earlier omission best explains it?
choices: She invited upward criticism too early, so the act of receiving made the pressure worse.
She never named the predictable strain that makes her react, so no safeguard existed when it returned.
She used a routine instead of trusting personal steadiness, so the process created distance during the hard exchange.
questions.explanation: The missing step is self-awareness about the failure point. The routine answer sounds human, but routines protect against strain.

reviewCards.front: When a tools section begins, what should come before scripts?
reviewCards.back: Build trust through a repeatable relationship habit. Later candor can only carry the strain that the relationship has capacity to bear.

reviewCards.front: What does get before you give require?
reviewCards.back: Ask for criticism about your own behavior before offering correction. Receiving first lowers hierarchy and makes candor reciprocal.

reviewCards.front: Why does staying centered belong in relationship work?
reviewCards.back: Your state is not private once it shapes how others experience your power. A centering habit keeps strain from becoming defensiveness.

reviewCards.front: What does a bad-day prompt reveal?
reviewCards.back: It names the pattern that makes you less able to bring your best self to work. Once named, the pattern can get a safeguard.

reviewCards.front: How do direct reports learn to trust you?
reviewCards.back: Through repeated evidence they can observe. Intentions and titles are too cheap; the other person needs proof that shows up in behavior.

reviewCards.front: Why does the relationship move travel across cultures?
reviewCards.back: Because it is a behavior, not a script: receive criticism first, stay centered, and build visible trust. The work has spread widely in translation, but the portable piece is the repeatable move, not the wording.

reviewCards.front: Why not wait until a performance problem appears?
reviewCards.back: Pressure makes first trust signals harder to believe. Build the relationship capacity before later tools raise the stakes.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Price The Trust Signal. Before you ask for candor, name the behavior that makes your ask less costly to answer. If the price is all on the other person, receive first and make the promise smaller. Trust grows through proof another person can see.

ifThenPlans.context: You want to offer advice to someone with less power.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I want to offer advice to someone with less power, then I count 1 criticism I have requested about my own behavior and ask it before advising.

ifThenPlans.context: You feel strained before a hard exchange.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I feel strained before a hard exchange, then I measure 5 minutes of centering before I reply.

ifThenPlans.context: A trust claim sounds too broad.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a trust claim sounds too broad, then I count 1 visible behavior that would prove it this week.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Replace one advice-first reply with a 10-minute read-aloud request: ask for one hard truth about your own behavior before you offer any counsel.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For 10 minutes each Friday, say aloud: "I asked for hard truth before I advised. I stayed centered by __. I showed trust by __." Write the blank you missed most.

memorableLines.text: Every advice-first habit charges trust before anyone has a chance to earn it.
What has Theodore done that makes hard truth less costly for Lucy?
Price the trust signal before you ask for candor.

chapters.title: Guidance
chapters.hook: Direct feedback can help. Everyone agreed; the receiver still paid for careless delivery.
chapters.counterintuition: Directness gets safer when it accepts limits. HHIPP keeps a true message from crossing the wrong line on timing, place, tone, and identity.
chapters.tryThisNow: Cross out one character label in a draft, then say aloud: "When you did X, Y happened; can we look at that?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use HHIPP before feedback leaves your mouth: be humble and helpful, act fast, go face to face, keep criticism private, and name behavior rather than character.

breakdown.fastRead:
Direct feedback can help. Everyone agreed; no one knew how to bring back proof without leaving a bruise. The Center for Creative Leadership, the group behind SBI, gives one plain way through it: name the Situation, the Behavior, and the Impact. Small misses travel.

SBI, a Situation, Behavior, Impact method, keeps the line tied to what was seen. HHIPP, the Humble, Helpful, Immediate, In Person, Private, and not Personalized list, guards the delivery. Helpful means useful to the other person, not satisfying to you. Use the list before the sentence leaves your mouth.

The promise holds only on a short clock. Immediate means 2-3 minutes when the context is fresh, not saving the line for later. Private means criticism does not need an audience. Not Personalized means the behavior gets named, not the person's worth.
breakdown.deepRead:
Center for Creative Leadership SBI slows the first impulse just enough to make it usable. You do not start with "you are careless." You start with where it happened, what the person did, and what effect followed. That small route matters because the speaker can be direct without turning the other person into the problem. The sentence travels on facts, not heat.

HHIPP adds the delivery risks SBI does not carry by itself. Humble keeps you open to being partly wrong. Helpful asks whether the line can aid the recipient. Immediate keeps the event close, so memory has not blurred. In Person keeps tone from going thin. Private lowers status threat for criticism. Not Personalized keeps identity out of the charge.

What risk is this member guarding? The answer changes with the miss. A public correction may show standards, but the crowd can turn learning into shame. A late note may sound calm, but the link to the act may be gone. A character label may feel crisp, but it spends trust and buys a fight.

CORE, a Context, Observation, Result, Explore flow from the Radical Candor team (the source group named with CORE), adds one more turn. Explore means the receiver can add facts and help shape what happens after the line lands. That is where a verdict becomes a talk. Directness gets safer when the other side can answer.

The checklist is not a shield for rude speed. It is a ledger. Six risks go out, six balances come back: humility, help, timing, presence, privacy, and behavior. Miss one, and the true part of the message may still fail.
breakdown.fullRead:
A checklist can make directness sound easy, which is exactly where it can fail. If you use HHIPP as a pass to fire off every true thought, the list has become a mask. The six members are not there to make you feel brave. They are there to keep the receiver able to learn.

Center for Creative Leadership SBI shows the first guardrail. Situation answers where and when. Behavior answers what was seen. Impact answers what changed because of it. The method is plain, but it blocks the leap from one act to a whole person. You can say, "In the handoff, the client file moved late, and the queue stalled," without saying, "You are lazy." One line can cross a lot of ground.

HHIPP then asks whether the line should move now, where it should land, and what it should leave untouched. Immediate does not mean blurting in the hallway. It means 2-3 minutes while the facts still sit near the act. In Person does not mean dragging someone into a show. It means tone and care can be read. Private means criticism is not made heavier by status loss.

Praise can be public because the status effect helps. Criticism is different. The audience changes the lesson into a display, and the recipient must now manage both the content and the social hit. If the aim is learning, privacy is not softness. It is the route that lets the useful part arrive.

Not Personalized is the member many people skip when they feel sure. Character words are fast. Careless, lazy, defensive, and sloppy all give the speaker a clean villain. They also trap the other person inside a trait. Behavior words keep change possible. What was done? What happened because of it? What can move now?

CORE brings the line back to dialogue. Context, Observation, and Result are close kin to SBI, but Explore matters because the speaker may not have the whole ledger. The receiver may know a fact the speaker missed. The receiver may accept the effect but see a better repair. Without Explore, the promise comes back as a verdict, and verdicts make people defend before they think.

The go-to question works on the same rule from the other side. A repeated prompt for direct reports makes upward criticism less vague. If you ask, "Any feedback?" the door is wide and easy to dodge. If you ask the same concrete question often, people know which path to take. The proof comes after you are criticized, not before.

Rewarding criticism closes the loop. A private thank-you may be kind, but people watch for visible proof that candor mattered. What changed after the hard line was said? If nothing moves, the ledger does not balance. The next honest person may decide silence is cheaper.

This can help even without title power. You can use SBI on your own promises, peer notes, and handoffs. You can cross out a character word before you send a message. You can ask for one clear critique and then show what changed. Guidance is not rank. Guidance is care made specific enough to be used.

Use the opposite move when safety, law, or urgent command needs a clear order. Do not Explore while a risk is still live and seconds matter. Do not make a private criticism public to prove nerve. Do not soften a fact until it vanishes. The list helps when the person can learn from the line; it fails when you use it to dodge a needed call or to dress up a blow.

examples.title: HHIPP Skipped at the Standard
examples.scenario: A team lead has a true criticism ready and the standard in hand: HHIPP names six members, including not Personalized, and directness alone does not qualify. She skips the list. The criticism lands in the open room, days late, aimed at character. The receiver hears a status hit before hearing the behavior that could change.
examples.whatToDo: Read the cost before you speak: move the criticism private, make it quick enough to link to the act, and cross out the character label.
examples.whyItMatters: Skipping HHIPP spends more than it saves. Truth without delivery care can buy shame, delay, and defense instead of change.

examples.title: SBI Pulls Back the Impression
examples.scenario: Center for Creative Leadership SBI is already in use when the line starts to drift. The speaker has said the effect, but the middle is still a general impression. The miss is close: "careless" would settle the matter too broadly. Situation and Behavior pull the sentence back before Impact turns into blame.
examples.whatToDo: The sentence works because SBI forces the speaker to pass through where, what, and effect before the judgment can harden.
examples.whyItMatters: The method pays off by making the feedback verifiable. A general impression can be denied; a seen act can be changed.

examples.title: CORE Leaves the Door Open
examples.scenario: What keeps a verdict from staying a verdict? On the call, the Radical Candor team's CORE reaches the return point at Explore. Context, Observation, and Result have been named, and the earlier commitment is now answered by the receiver's turn. The speaker does not yet know what facts will come back or whether the repair will hold.
examples.whatToDo: The question opens the answer: after Context, Observation, and Result, ask the receiver what else needs to be known.
examples.whyItMatters: The turn keeps feedback from becoming a one-way sentence. Explore lets missing facts enter before the repair moves.

examples.title: SBI Pays the Cost
examples.scenario: Center for Creative Leadership SBI has already done its job, and the folded page shows the cost. The speaker gave up the quick label, named the situation, named the behavior, and kept impact tied to what changed. The line took longer. The receiver got something usable.
examples.whatToDo: The page says: pay the cost of detail before you name the effect.
examples.whyItMatters: The trade is clear: less speed, more change.

examples.title: The Direct Report Sees Proof
examples.scenario: HHIPP first reaches the direct report on the call after the go-to question has been asked; the 2-3 minutes after criticism will decide whether the answer counts. Private thanks alone is heading for a miss. Visible reward pulls it back: the criticized behavior changes, so future candor has proof.
examples.whatToDo: The proof must be visible: ask the same clear prompt, thank the person, and show one change that came from the criticism.
examples.whyItMatters: The witness is downstream. Reward criticism where people can see it, or the next true line may never leave the sender.

questions.prompt: A trainer turns HHIPP into a broad culture slogan for every trust issue. What is actually wrong with that use?
choices: The trainer is applying HHIPP too late, after feedback has already lost its context.
The trainer is using a delivery checklist as if it were a general culture label.
The trainer is skipping Private, because turning the list into a slogan makes every criticism public.
questions.explanation: HHIPP belongs to feedback mechanics, not every culture problem. It is a delivery checklist, so treating it as a wide slogan stretches the tool beyond its job.

questions.prompt: During a standup, a lead wants to correct one person so the standard is clear. Which choice fits HHIPP?
choices: Save both praise and criticism for a later private conversation so no peer can compare status.
Correct the person in front of peers, then soften the status hit with a helpful tone.
Move criticism private, while allowing praise to stay public when it helps the person.
questions.explanation: Private guards against turning criticism into shame. The public-standard choice is tempting, but the audience adds status threat and can block learning.

questions.prompt: Your draft is true and direct, but it ignores delivery risks. Which revision uses the full HHIPP guardrail?
choices: Keep the message direct if the facts are sound, then fix tone only if the receiver objects.
Make the line humble and helpful, but leave timing and privacy for later judgment.
Make it humble, helpful, quick, face to face, private for criticism, and aimed at behavior.
questions.explanation: The full list matters because each member guards a different risk. A true line can still fail if timing, privacy, or identity language is skipped.

questions.prompt: A peer says, "You seemed off all morning," and cannot name what happened. What is the best next move?
choices: State where it happened, what was observed, and what changed so the claim can be checked.
Ask whether the peer has enough proof to make the same impression public and hard to dispute.
Delay the comment until a formal review gives the impression more weight.
questions.explanation: SBI forces observable specificity. The proof choice still leaves a general impression in charge; the useful move is to name where, what, and effect.

questions.prompt: When your direct reports keep dodging upward criticism, which request lowers the ambiguity?
choices: Ask for any thoughts whenever people seem ready, so the request keeps a broad scope.
Use the same go-to question so people know exactly how to criticize upward.
Wait for stronger evidence that people want to speak before asking again.
questions.explanation: A repeated prompt gives people a clear path. A vague open request sounds kind, but it is easy to dodge because no one knows what kind of critique is wanted.

questions.prompt: A note says, "You are lazy with handoffs," though the missed act is clear. Which principle does it break?
choices: It uses the right behavior focus but sends the message after context has faded.
It attacks character instead of naming behavior and impact that can change.
It makes the criticism private when praise would have been better in public.
questions.explanation: Not Personalized keeps the person out of the charge. The timing answer is a near miss only if delay is the issue; here the identity label is the break.

questions.prompt: After a direct report criticizes your choice, you thank them in private and change nothing. What happens downstream?
choices: Future honesty gets less safe because people see no proof that candor mattered.
The private thanks is enough because reward works best when no one else sees it.
The criticism should wait for a later review so the reaction can feel less tense.
questions.explanation: People watch the reaction to criticism. Private thanks may sound respectful, but without visible reward or change, the ledger teaches silence.

questions.prompt: In a feedback talk, Context, Observation, and Result are clear. Which move keeps it from becoming a one-way verdict?
choices: Add Explore so the receiver can add facts and help shape what comes after.
Stop after Result, since extra discussion may weaken the feedback and blur the point.
Move back to Situation and Behavior to make the first claim more exact.
questions.explanation: Explore invites dialogue after the observed result is named. Repeating earlier parts may add detail, but it still can leave the receiver outside the repair.

questions.prompt: A supervisor stores every criticism for a scheduled review so the wording can be cleaner. What is the likely cost?
choices: The feedback may become too private for the recipient to connect it with behavior.
The criticism may sound too humble, so the standard will be hard to hear.
The context can fade, making the person less able to link the line to the act.
questions.explanation: Immediate means close to the behavior, often within 2-3 minutes. Waiting for a later review can make the act harder to recall and use.

reviewCards.front: What are the six HHIPP members, and why do they belong together?
reviewCards.back: HHIPP means Humble, Helpful, Immediate, In Person, Private, and not Personalized. They belong together because directness needs delivery limits, not just true content.

reviewCards.front: How does SBI stop feedback from becoming a vague impression?
reviewCards.back: SBI makes the speaker name the Situation, the Behavior, and the Impact. That keeps the line tied to what was observed instead of a mood about the person.

reviewCards.front: What does not Personalized require you to remove from criticism?
reviewCards.back: Remove character labels. Name the act and its effect instead, because identity attacks make defense more likely while behavior language leaves room for change.

reviewCards.front: Why does CORE add Explore after Context, Observation, and Result?
reviewCards.back: Explore gives the receiver a turn. They can add missing facts and help shape what happens after the feedback, so the line does not stay a one-way verdict.

reviewCards.front: Why does a repeated go-to question work better than a vague request for feedback?
reviewCards.back: The repeated prompt lowers ambiguity. People know what kind of upward criticism is wanted, while a broad request is easy to dodge without seeming unhelpful.

reviewCards.front: What proof do people need after they criticize upward?
reviewCards.back: They need visible reward that candor mattered. Thanks helps, but future honesty gets safer when people can see a real response or change.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Cross-Out Careless Feedback. Before you say or send criticism, remove one word that judges the person and replace it with the observed behavior and effect. Then check timing and privacy so the line can be heard.

ifThenPlans.context: If your draft uses a character word like lazy, careless, or defensive
ifThenPlans.plan: If the draft names a trait, then cross out that word and write the situation, behavior, and impact instead.

ifThenPlans.context: If the behavior just happened and the facts are still fresh
ifThenPlans.plan: If the moment is still clear, then give the line in 2-3 minutes rather than storing it for later.

ifThenPlans.context: If criticism would land in front of an audience
ifThenPlans.plan: If people are watching, then move the criticism private and keep any public comment for praise.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Spend 5 minutes today: cross out one character label and pre-write one exact sentence to say or send, using behavior plus impact.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Audit three feedback drafts for timing, privacy, and character labels before they leave.

memorableLines.text: Use the list before the sentence leaves your mouth.
The proof comes after you are criticized, not before.
Helpful means useful to the other person, not satisfying to you.

chapters.title: Team
chapters.hook: Why did analyst Spencer's career help almost point him at the wrong role?
chapters.counterintuition: Career help gets more personal when it gets more structured. The sequence keeps group lead Vera from treating Spencer's old ambition as today's map.
chapters.tryThisNow: Move one calendar block toward a Career Conversation and count the minutes it protects. Record that single number before you give career advice.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Run Career Conversations as a sequence: learn past choices, ask for several futures, then turn one dream into learning for the next 6-18 months.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why did analyst Spencer's career help almost point him at the wrong role? Vera began with the role, not the person. Career Conversations use three talks. Life Story looks back at key choices. Dreams asks for several possible futures. The Eighteen-Month Plan names skills to learn over 6-18 months.

Each talk has its own job. The old map looked useful. It almost failed because Spencer's aims had changed while Vera was still steering from last year's answer to the current role talk. One quick chat would have mixed his history, hopes, and skill need into one thin answer.

Care gets concrete here. Vera owes Spencer discovery before advice: what has pulled him before, what futures he can name, and what skill should move now. Whose old ambition are you still using as today's map?
breakdown.deepRead:
Three talks slow the guess at three points. Russ Laraway, credited for Career Conversations, matters here for one reason: the tool has an order. The source gives three roughly 45-minute talks, not one warm chat. A single chat spends the past, future, and learning path in one rushed pile.

Life Story, the first talk, looks at choices during key changes. Vera does not start by asking Spencer what promotion he wants. She asks where his own choices kept pulling him. Repeated choices expose motive better than a title wish. Care is not a mood here; it is the act of learning what the person wants before you steer.

Use the sequence when the person can still reflect and choose. Do not use it to hide from a fit call that has already failed despite real effort. The same care extends to hiring and firing. Care can mean a better path, but it can also mean saying the current role is wrong.

Dreams, the second talk, asks for 3-5 visions. That plural part matters. One future can sound neat while it hides the thing that actually pulls the person. When Spencer names several futures, Vera can hear which aims repeat and which are just borrowed from the org chart. The map gets less false.

The Eighteen-Month Plan, the third talk, turns a dream into learning over 6-18 months. Vera owes Spencer the skill, not just praise for his ambition. If he needs a new skill, who owes him the chance to learn it, and by when? The loop closes only when a near step exists.
breakdown.fullRead:
Without title power, you can still use the sequence on your own promises. Ask what past choices kept pulling you, name several futures, then pick one skill to learn in the next 6-18 months. That is not a full staffing tool when you have no hiring power. It is still a way to stop old goals from steering new choices.

Spencer's case turns on a plain miss. Vera thought she was helping by asking about the role first. That sounds efficient. It also smuggles in a guess: last year's ambition still holds. People's goals and constraints change, so last year's answer is not a standing order. A career map is a fresh read, not a stored label.

Russ Laraway's Career Conversations run as three conversations of about 45 minutes each. The order protects each answer from swallowing the others. Life Story keeps the talk from becoming ladder talk too soon. Dreams keeps one narrow future from closing the field. The Eighteen-Month Plan keeps hope from ending as a kind speech with no skill attached. Each pass owes a different answer.

Career Conversations are a way of making care visible. Generic concern cannot tell Vera which learning chance Spencer needs. It cannot tell Spencer why the old role no longer fits. It cannot tell Suzanne whether a staffing promise rests on a live aim or an old guess. The loop that closes is simple: past pull, several futures, near learning.

There is a staffing edge too. The Team prompts link this unit to the balance of rock stars and superstars, the source's names for stability and stretch. Do not turn that line into a race for speed. A healthy group needs people who hold knowledge and people who press into new skill. If everyone is treated as if fast promotion is the only win, continuity gets spent.

The hard edge is fit. If Ryder has tried and the role still does not fit, Vera cannot make care mean keeping every person in place. Career Conversations may reveal a new learning path. They may also reveal that the current seat is wrong. Kindness without clarity can leave a person stuck while the group absorbs the cost.

The sequence also guards against borrowed certainty. A senior voice may remember what Spencer wanted last year. A guide may give the order. Neither can replace the live answer. Vera still owes Spencer the talks, and Spencer still owes himself a current map. Structure does not make the choice for them; it keeps their guesses from pretending to be facts.

What should move first? Not a role promise. Not a pep talk. Move the discovery. Ask for the transition choices before the title wish. Ask for 3-5 futures before the single path. Ask for one learning step before you praise the dream. Then write who owes whom what by when.

A career map is not a ladder drawn once; it is the loop that closes before the miss. It fails when Vera rushes it into one chat or uses it to delay a hard fit call. It works when Spencer leaves with a current read of himself and a near skill to learn. The map must be live.

examples.title: The Old Map Almost Wins
examples.scenario: Analyst Spencer had already left the staffing huddle when group lead Vera asked the question the reader would ask: why did the old path almost win? The blue folder lay shut. She traced it back to the first pass. Before Life Story, before Dreams or the 6-18 months, she had treated last year's ambition as fixed. After key transitions, the old role looked less like a fit and more like a stale map.
examples.whatToDo: What would skipping Life Story cost? Vera would steer from an old map. Start with key transitions before any role advice hardens.
examples.whyItMatters: The price is a near miss. Repeated choices tell Vera what has pulled Spencer, while a title wish may only repeat an old answer.

examples.title: Suzanne Feels the Futures
examples.scenario: Operations partner Suzanne first feels the effect at the staffing huddle when Spencer's 3-5 visions in Dreams make Vera pause the assignment. One future points to the role Suzanne expected him to take; another points away from it. "So we do not know yet," Suzanne says. "Not from one future," Vera answers. The staffing call waits, and no one knows whether the open role will still fit.
examples.whatToDo: Old stories cost Suzanne a clean staffing call. Ask for several futures before naming one slot, then wait until the learning need is clear.
examples.whyItMatters: A narrow dream keeps the old path in charge. Several visions show whether the role is a true pull or only the neat answer.

examples.title: The Learning Step Appears
examples.scenario: Analyst Spencer's Eighteen-Month Plan still did not add up after Life Story and Dreams: the 6-18 months were named, but no skill had moved. Vera caught it in the staffing huddle before anyone called the talks complete. A dry marker squeaked. She gave up the fast promise of a bigger role and named the learning step first. Spencer left with less certainty and more traction.
examples.whatToDo: Drift costs Spencer months. Name the skill before you praise the dream, and move one current task toward learning it now.
examples.whyItMatters: Encouragement feels kind but can leave the path empty. A near learning step gives care a shape Spencer can act on this week.

examples.title: The Fit Call Stays Hard
examples.scenario: Group lead Vera stated the demand during the staffing huddle. "If fit has failed after effort, care cannot mean keeping the seat frozen." Project partner Ryder wanted one more stretch chance; Suzanne needed stability; Spencer's learning path was still live. The Team prompts on rock stars and superstars, plus hiring and firing, helped them stop idolizing speed. They still did not know whether Ryder's current role was wrong.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the hard fit standard and Vera can rename delay as care. Compare stability, stretch, and mismatch before keeping a role in place.
examples.whyItMatters: Keeping everyone can cost clarity. The prompt half-works if it names speed and stability but still dodges the actual fit call.

questions.prompt: Last year, a designer wanted a larger client role. This year, her lead skips discovery and assigns that path again. Which principle breaks?
choices: The lead runs the full sequence only after the client role fails, so discovery becomes a late repair instead of a current read.
The lead follows a senior person's memory of the old answer, so rank replaces what the designer can say now.
The lead treats an old ambition as fixed, instead of checking how the person's path has changed.
questions.explanation: The failure is using last year's answer as today's map. The senior-memory choice is tempting, but the core issue is stale discovery, not who remembered it.

questions.prompt: In a college club, a mentor asks one volunteer for a single five-year target and builds all help around it. What should change?
choices: Keep the single target until the club role settles, because volunteer help needs one answer before support can start.
Ask for 3-5 possible futures first, so the volunteer can show aims that do not fit one narrow lane.
Move to a learning step right away, because future talk can wait until the club has a role to fill.
questions.explanation: Dreams stays plural on purpose. The learning-step choice sounds active, but it jumps ahead before the volunteer has named more than one possible future.

questions.prompt: A new lead says career help will be casual encouragement plus a few check-ins when schedules allow. What is the violation?
choices: The lead starts with care language but waits for a staffing crunch before asking about growth in the first serious talk.
The lead asks the most senior peer to bless the approach, as if authority can replace the method.
The lead treats a named sequence as loose support, instead of running the specific Career Conversations.
questions.explanation: The tool is credited and documented as a sequence, so loose encouragement is not enough. The senior-peer option borrows authority but still misses the structure.

questions.prompt: After months of real effort, a role still does not fit and the lead keeps the person only to seem caring. Why does the problem persist?
choices: Care has been split from fit, so the hard personnel call is avoided even when the mismatch remains.
The lead began career talks too early, before the person had enough tenure to discuss fit with useful detail.
The lead should wait for a named source to settle the call, so personal judgment does not enter.
questions.explanation: Role fit can fail despite effort. Waiting for more tenure sounds patient, but the stem says effort has already happened and the mismatch remains.

questions.prompt: A supervisor hears a designer name a dream role, starts to praise it, and wants the talk to lead somewhere before the assignment changes. Which action comes first?
choices: Celebrate the dream and leave skill steps for a later staffing cycle, so the person's interest stays intact.
Name the skill to learn in the coming 6-18 months, so the dream gets a near path.
Ask for several more dream roles, even after the pattern is clear, so no one narrows too soon.
questions.explanation: The near-term learning step turns a dream into action. Asking for more dreams can be useful earlier, but it overextends the prior pass here.

questions.prompt: A lead says she cares about an employee but cannot name what has ever pulled him toward good work. Why does the claim feel thin?
choices: She starts the sequence only when a role opens, so care depends on staffing timing instead of the employee's own story.
She has not learned the person's own motives or possible futures, so concern has no useful shape.
She asks the person to choose one future, so care becomes too tidy to guide a conversation.
questions.explanation: Career Conversations make care concrete by learning motives and dreams. The single-future answer is related, but the stem shows no discovery at all.

questions.prompt: Your study group rewards only members who take harder parts each week, while steady experts keep the basics from slipping. What maps from this lesson?
choices: Look at the mix of stretch and stability, because a healthy group needs more than promotion-speed behavior.
Push everyone toward the harder parts, because shared stretch proves the group is developing faster than stable expertise can.
Let the group's oldest member decide the mix, because status can stand in for reading the actual roles.
questions.explanation: The guide's balance points to mix, not one idolized mode. The shared-stretch choice sounds ambitious, but it spends the stability the group needs.

questions.prompt: A lead has calendar pressure and tries to cover past choices, future hopes, and learning in one quick career chat. What breaks?
choices: The distinct purposes get flattened, so one chat cannot hear history, possible futures, and learning well.
The lead asks for 3-5 futures too early, so a plural dream list replaces any career talk about past choices.
The lead should let the employee choose the order alone, because structure would reduce candor.
questions.explanation: The three roughly 45-minute talks protect different purposes. The plural-futures answer uses a real piece, but timing is not the failure in this stem.

questions.prompt: Before asking which promotion an employee wants, what should a lead ask about first?
choices: Ask which title the person wants least, so the ladder is ruled out before growth begins and no promotion target dominates.
Ask a senior colleague which path looks likely, so outside standing checks the answer.
Ask about key transition choices, so repeated patterns show what has actually energized the person.
questions.explanation: Life Story starts with choices at key transitions. Asking a senior colleague may sound practical, but it swaps the person's pattern for outside standing.

reviewCards.front: What makes Career Conversations more than casual encouragement?
reviewCards.back: They are a credited sequence with three roughly 45-minute talks. Treat them as a method: past choices, several futures, then near learning.

reviewCards.front: Why start with Life Story before asking about a desired role?
reviewCards.back: Life Story looks at choices during key transitions. Repeated choices reveal what has energized the person better than a quick role wish.

reviewCards.front: What does asking for 3-5 Dreams protect against?
reviewCards.back: It keeps one narrow future from hiding the real pull. Several visions loosen the assumption that growth must mean one corporate path.

reviewCards.front: What must come out of the Eighteen-Month Plan?
reviewCards.back: A learning step for the next 6-18 months. The dream should connect to a skill, not end as praise or a vague promise.

reviewCards.front: Why should an old ambition not steer a current career choice by itself?
reviewCards.back: A person's path is dynamic. Goals and constraints change, so the current map has to be discovered again instead of copied from last year.

reviewCards.front: When does caring about growth require a harder staffing call?
reviewCards.back: When role fit fails despite effort. Development can mean stretch or stability, but care can also require clarity that the current role is wrong.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Move One Learning Step. Start with the person's past choices, ask for several futures, then move one current task toward the skill needed in the next 6-18 months. The skill is not encouragement; it is turning a career talk into a learning action.

ifThenPlans.context: First a person names a desired role; then advice starts to form.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the role name appears before Life Story, then move back to two key transitions before discussing the role.

ifThenPlans.context: First several futures surface; then one skill keeps showing up.
ifThenPlans.plan: If one skill appears across several futures, then move the talk toward the first chance to learn it.

ifThenPlans.context: First the role fit still fails; then kindness starts to mean delay.
ifThenPlans.plan: If effort has not fixed the mismatch, then move from encouragement to the clear fit conversation.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Spend 20 minutes moving one vague career promise into one learning step for the next 6-18 months.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: If a career ask comes up this week, then pause before advice and ask which part is missing: past choices, several futures, or near learning.

memorableLines.text: Care is not a mood here; it is the act of learning what the person wants before you steer.
A single chat spends the past, future, and learning path in one rushed pile.
Whose old ambition are you still using as today's map?

chapters.title: Results
chapters.hook: You write one more recurring invite, and the hour it steals is the hour the task needed.
chapters.counterintuition: Results gets softer and stricter at once. You do not prove care by adding time together; you prove it by naming the job and cutting what steals execution.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write a 10-minute job line for the recurring invite most likely to steal execution time.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Turn collaboration into routines with one test: each recurring slot must protect listening, idea care, debate, decision, or execution, and vague slots get cut.

breakdown.fastRead:
You are writing one more recurring invite when the Results question lands: what is this slot for? Results is where the framework cashes out, in getting things done together without eating the week. Its demands are concrete: 1:1 time, new ideas, staff time, Big Debate, Big Decision, total load, and creep risk.

A 1:1 is recurring time for the direct report's priorities. Big Debate tests an idea before people commit. Big Decision is the separate place where the choice closes. Creep risk is the slow spread of recurring slots until execution has no air.

The rule is plain. Write the purpose, then guard the slot. Who pays when a calendar says yes to every invite? The person who needed the hour to do the task pays first.
breakdown.deepRead:
Results prompts work because they put two questions in tension. What kind of collaboration does this slot protect, and what execution does it steal? You need both questions. One without the other makes a crowded calendar.

Meeting architecture means giving each recurring slot one job. The Results prompts name the jobs. Listen in 1:1s. Give new ideas a place before full debate. Keep staff time from becoming a catch-all. Test ideas in Big Debate, and close choices in Big Decision. That is the split side of the lesson. It keeps raw ideas from being judged too soon, and it keeps debate from dragging on after a choice is due.

Meeting creep pushes from the other side. It starts when each concern earns one more invite. That can feel kind, because no voice is left out and no risk is rushed. It is costly. Every unpriced invite asks someone to make up the lost execution later.

The 1:1 shows the price clearly. Radical Candor ties that practice to Creating Effective 1:1 Meetings and Meet Like a Boss. Use it as a status toll and the manager gets a fast scan, but direct reports lose the protected channel for priorities and obstacles. Use it for direct reports first, and the manager gives up speed for better guidance. Write the job before you protect the slot.

You can use this without rank. Ask which talk is for listening, which forum is for testing, and when the choice will close. If no one can answer, the routine is not aligned. It is only full.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hard case is not the useless slot. It is the useful slot that has started to lie. The 1:1 still has the right name, but status takes it over. The staff slot still looks normal, but it now holds idea care, debate, decisions, and updates. Big Debate has the right name, but someone tries to choose before the idea has been tested. Big Decision has the right name, but people reopen debate to avoid closure.

That is why Results and meeting creep belong in the same frame. Results prompts say: split the jobs so each kind of collaboration gets the conditions it needs. Creep says each split can become another claim on the same scarce execution time. Too few slots blur the job. Too many slots bury it.

So price the default. A 1:1 taken over by status costs the direct report a listening channel. Judging a raw idea in the same place where choices are made costs the group a thought that might have grown. Deciding before debate costs you a brittle commitment. Debating after the choice costs you a start. Waiting for formal cycles to guide performance costs the person a chance to change while the task is live.

Subtraction is part of the craft. A slot can be useful and still be too expensive this week. A question can deserve an answer and still not deserve a recurring invite. The test is plain: if cutting the slot would free execution without harming listening, idea care, debate, or choice, cut it. If cutting it would break one of those jobs, redesign it until the cost is clear.

Addition has a narrow place. If rough ideas have no safe forum, make one. If tested debate has no close, make one. Add only when the new slot buys back the job it names.

Ask smaller, sharper questions. Who is this for? What kind of task does it protect? What would get worse if we cut it? What would finally start if we redesigned it? These questions keep the tool open to people without title power. You can ask for your own 1:1 to start with your priority. You can ask whether a rough idea is being weighed too early. You can name the cost of one more recurring slot.

The move fails when the slot exists to dodge a harder act. If a choice is overdue, another debate is not brave. If guidance is needed now, a later formal cycle is not fair. If the calendar is full because no one wants to remove a ritual, one more invite is not care. Cut or redesign the slot that cannot name its job. Results do not sit after care; they test whether care can run.

examples.title: Prompt Names the Standard
examples.scenario: A program manager sits down with the week's calendar and holds every slot to the Results standard before anyone can defend a familiar invite. 1:1s, new ideas, staff time, Big Debate, Big Decision, total load, and meeting creep all need answers. The demand is not more talk. It is a calendar where each slot serves one collaboration job. The open problem remains: which current invite has no job?
examples.whatToDo: Ask which slot has no job. Write the purpose in one plain line, then reject any defense that only says people expect the invite.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask who pays. Price the vague invite as lost execution, then make someone name the listening, idea, debate, or decision job it protects.

examples.title: 1:1 Time Moves Back
examples.scenario: The status sweep is already off the 1:1 agenda. The manager gives up the fast scan and starts with the direct report's priority, as Creating Effective 1:1 Meetings and Meet Like a Boss point the slot toward the employee. The shared calendar invite still says 1:1. Its blue dot stays on the week. The cost is less control for the manager; the result is help close enough to change the task.
examples.whatToDo: What skipping this costs is the direct report's protected channel; move status elsewhere and begin with the employee's priority.
examples.whyItMatters: What the cost buys is earlier help: the manager loses a fast scan, but the employee gets room to name the priority while it can move.

examples.title: Decision Holds the Line
examples.scenario: The Big Decision forum convenes after Big Debate has done its job. The idea has been tested, and now the choice should close. A fresh concern tries to reopen the argument. The forum starts slipping until the risk is named as part of the choice, not as a reason to restart debate. The decision closes barely in time for execution to start.
examples.whatToDo: Why the split works: the test happened before the choice, so name the remaining risk and close instead of sending the group back to debate.
examples.whyItMatters: What fails without the split is timing. Debate too soon commits early; debate too late keeps execution waiting after the choice is due.

examples.title: Staff Time Swells
examples.scenario: Why did the staff slot swell after it was over? It had absorbed listening, idea care, debate, decisions, and status because each need felt too small for its own home. Meeting creep, the spread of recurring time into execution time, had already taken space. The trace is clear. The repair is not. The next calendar has not yet been cut.
examples.whatToDo: Which leak came first: the staff slot lost its single purpose. Split the jobs, then decide whether the ritual stays, shrinks, or ends.
examples.whyItMatters: Why the answer is not enough: naming the leak does not remove it, and delay keeps charging execution time for the same blur.

examples.title: Guidance Lands While Useful
examples.scenario: Meeting creep shows up during the current handoff, where the same delay appears for the third time while everyone is still trying to protect execution. The manager almost saves the note for the formal cycle, then stops beside the task instead. Results includes impromptu feedback frequency because guidance near execution can still move the work. The correction lands while the file is open, and the later review only records what already traveled.
examples.whatToDo: Give the note while the task can change. Keep the later formal cycle for evidence that has already reached the work, and do not let the number of meetings hide the missed guidance.
examples.whyItMatters: Late guidance can explain a miss, but it cannot improve the current result. Close feedback keeps meeting creep from turning execution trouble into review-season surprise.

examples.title: Calendar Loses Air
examples.scenario: The number of meetings looks harmless before anyone calls it a problem. More recurring slots were added to cure confusion, and execution time has less space. The risk needs a plain signal, not another invite. The week is a solid block of color. The creep is pulled back late when one slot from staff meetings is removed or redesigned before a new slot can be added.
examples.whatToDo: Ask where the air went. Count current recurring slots before adding one; remove or redesign the weakest old invite first today.
examples.whyItMatters: What must stay open is execution time. Guard it from good intent that keeps asking for another recurring invite today.

questions.prompt: A volunteer tutor has a standing 1:1 with a student, but keeps using it to gather updates for the program director. What maps from Results?
choices: Use the 1:1 for the student's priorities and obstacles before collecting updates elsewhere.
Keep the 1:1 focused on the director's report because rank sets the useful agenda.
Save the student's concerns for the end of term because a formal cycle is cleaner evidence.
questions.explanation: A 1:1 protects the other person's priorities. The director-focused choice borrows rank as proof, but it loses the listening channel the slot exists to guard.

questions.prompt: After a community board call fails, the recap shows updates, raw ideas, hard debate, and final choices all collided. Which earlier step was missing?
choices: Ask the chair to settle every item sooner so the board can move through the packed agenda.
Move the hardest item to a private 1:1, even though the failure involved the whole recurring group slot.
Give the recurring staff-style slot a clear job instead of letting it absorb every collaboration need.
questions.explanation: The failure is a catch-all staff slot. Asking the chair to push faster still leaves listening, debate, and choice blurred in the same place.

questions.prompt: When a school club kills each fresh idea during the same session where it votes on events, members stop bringing rough options. What is actually wrong?
choices: New ideas are being judged before they have a safer place to take shape.
The club should let the oldest member approve ideas before anyone else reacts.
The vote should happen even earlier so weak ideas stop taking group time.
questions.explanation: Young ideas need a place before full debate. Letting the oldest member decide only swaps premature judgment for borrowed authority.

questions.prompt: Your nonprofit says alignment is low, so it wants two more recurring calls. What should happen before another invite goes out?
choices: Copy the cadence used by a larger nonprofit because its size makes the model safer.
Ask the busiest volunteer which call feels least painful, then protect the rest for consistency.
Count the current calendar load against execution time and add only what earns its cost.
questions.explanation: The number of slots competes with doing time. Copying a larger group treats outside practice as proof instead of pricing the load here.

questions.prompt: The launch slipped because the group kept reopening argument after argument, and no one would close the choice. What caused the miss?
choices: The group skipped early idea care, so the proposal had no place to become clear before debate.
The group lacked a separate decision forum that would turn tested debate into closure.
The group asked for fewer updates, so status details stopped giving enough proof.
questions.explanation: The cause is endless debate where closure was needed. More early idea care would not fix a choice that already needs to close.

questions.prompt: Before a product change is tested, a senior sponsor wants the group to choose today so the launch can move. Which move fits the Results split?
choices: Let the sponsor decide now because senior rank can stand in for debate when time is tight.
Hold the idea in Big Debate first, so the group tests it before commitment.
Send the proposal straight to Big Decision, then treat later concerns as execution details.
questions.explanation: Big Debate protects friction before commitment. Senior rank may feel efficient, but it can close on an untested idea too soon.

questions.prompt: In a choir rehearsal, the director saves every correction for the seasonal written evaluation while singers keep repeating the same miss. Which Results move transfers best?
choices: Wait for the written evaluation because formal records carry better evidence than practice moments.
Ask the section lead to rank singers first, then give notes only to the weakest voice.
Give guidance near rehearsal while the singer can still change the current performance.
questions.explanation: Guidance close to the act can change current performance. The formal-record choice arrives too late to shape the singing now.

questions.prompt: A supervisor under deadline treats Results as pressure added after relationship work, then wonders why the routines feel punitive. What is the cold diagnosis?
choices: The supervisor should set care aside because routines matter more once output is due.
The supervisor is missing that Results turns collaboration into routines for how work gets done.
The supervisor should cite the most senior process owner and follow that person's cadence.
questions.explanation: Results is not pressure tacked on after care. It turns collaboration into routine, while the senior-process answer outsources the judgment.

questions.prompt: After a design studio adds a recurring sync to cure overload, makers ship less and the calendar fills again. Which earlier move would have helped?
choices: Remove or redesign an existing recurring slot before adding another one to the calendar.
Keep the new sync but aim it at the makers who already have the least execution time to spare.
Accept the full calendar as proof that people are aligned enough to ship soon.
questions.explanation: Calendar creep deepens the bottleneck when overload is solved with another slot. Targeting makers with less time worsens the same cost.

reviewCards.front: What should a 1:1 protect before it becomes a status sweep?
reviewCards.back: It should protect the direct report's priorities and current obstacles. Status can be gathered elsewhere, but protected listening is hard to recover once the slot is spent.

reviewCards.front: Why do rough ideas need a place before full debate?
reviewCards.back: Early ideas can be useful before they are strong. If they are judged in the same place where choices are made, they may die before the group learns what they could become.

reviewCards.front: How do Big Debate and Big Decision split the job?
reviewCards.back: Big Debate tests an idea before commitment. Big Decision closes the choice after that testing, so argument does not stay open forever and execution can begin.

reviewCards.front: How can staff time become a trap?
reviewCards.back: It becomes a trap when it absorbs listening, idea care, debate, decisions, and updates at once. The label stays familiar, but the purpose blurs.

reviewCards.front: What should happen before adding another recurring invite?
reviewCards.back: Ask what execution time the new slot will take and whether an existing slot can be removed or redesigned. More time together is not the same as better alignment.

reviewCards.front: Why does frequent impromptu feedback belong with Results?
reviewCards.back: Feedback close to the task can change the result while it is still being made. Waiting for a formal cycle turns guidance into late commentary.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Write the Calendar Job. Put one plain job beside a recurring invite before you defend it. If the job is listening, debate, decision, idea care, or guidance, protect the conditions it needs; if the job is vague, cut or redesign the slot.

ifThenPlans.context: If a 1:1 starts with your status questions
ifThenPlans.plan: If the status sweep comes first, then say, "This slot starts with your priority; I will ask for status after that."

ifThenPlans.context: If debate keeps reopening after a choice is due
ifThenPlans.plan: If the argument returns past the deadline, then say, "We tested the idea; now we are naming the risk and closing the choice."

ifThenPlans.context: If overload tempts you to add another recurring invite
ifThenPlans.plan: If the new invite is already drafted, then say, "We cut or redesign one old slot before we add a new one."

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Audit one existing calendar invite for 15 minutes: write its job, who it serves, and what execution time it protects.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, observe where a recurring slot blurred listening, debate, decision, or doing; note the one invite you will cut or redesign.

memorableLines.text: Who pays when a calendar says yes to every invite?
Write the job before you protect the slot.
Results do not sit after care; they test whether care can run.

chapters.title: A Radically Candid Performance Review
chapters.hook: A fair review can still fail when the person hears the hard truth too late.
chapters.counterintuition: The formal cycle is not where candor gets stronger by saving it up. It gets stronger when the cycle counts what already traveled, with no score allowed to replace guidance.
chapters.tryThisNow: When you draft a rating sentence, say the prior guidance it should summarize in 10 words before you keep it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat the formal cycle as a ledger: it counts guidance already given, keeps scores from crowding out growth, and turns evidence into shared next steps.

breakdown.fastRead:
A fair review can fail when the score lands after the chance to change. The person sees a verdict, not a path. That is the Measurement Problem: measurement can pull attention toward a score and away from learning.

Radical Candor gives the formal review its own treatment, A Radically Candid Performance Review, past the daily tools. The questions are practical: do the formal performance review elements work, and do development conversations happen with everyone before the rating cycle?

Use the cycle as a ledger. Each promise out needs a return path. Evidence comes from what was seen and what changed. The hard truth should have traveled earlier. If it first arrives here, the process has a debt.
breakdown.deepRead:
The score pulls because it feels final. Once a number is in play, the person being rated may stop hearing the lesson and start reading the odds. The Measurement Problem names that split as Development Versus Management: learning needs a path, while management decisions carry power.

A formal performance review is the set process an organization uses to rate and record performance. The bonus prompts do not tell you to copy one form. They ask what your elements are and whether they work. That is motion and ledger at once: trace where the promise traveled, then count what the process made visible.

Evidence keeps the line from becoming a label. SBI means Situation, Behavior, Impact: where it happened, what was seen, and what changed because of it. CORE means Context, Observation, Result, Explore: the setting, the seen act, the result, and a prompt that brings the employee into the path ahead.

Who pays for surprise? The person who could have changed earlier pays first. The person writing the cycle pays too, because trust drops when a score carries news that should have traveled sooner. A candid cycle does not hide the hard part. It just refuses to store it until the last mile.

A score may still be needed. Pay, role scope, and record keeping do not vanish. But the score should not pose as growth. Development talks need room to ask what behavior returns on what path. Management calls need care because money and status change how honest people can be.
breakdown.fullRead:
The formal review changes the job. The everyday tools run while the work can still move; A Radically Candid Performance Review asks how those tools behave when a formal system starts counting. A rating cycle can help a person see a pattern. It can also make one number look like the whole truth.

Start with the process, not the person. What elements does it use? Do they help? Do development conversations happen with everyone before the cycle closes? These prompts move your eyes from blame to design. If the form rewards vague praise and late criticism, a careful writer still has a bad rail to travel.

That does not excuse weak guidance. It locates the debt. Had the hard detail not traveled earlier, the formal cycle would ask the reader to accept a verdict without a chance to improve. Had the score been treated as development, the person would know where they ranked but not what to do on Monday.

Behavior evidence repairs part of that harm. SBI keeps the line tied to a situation, a behavior, and its impact. CORE adds the Explore step, so the employee can add context and help shape the return path. Unless both sides can name that path, the promise thins into good intentions.

The half-fix is common. A person may gather clean evidence and still run the hour as a one-way verdict. That is why Explore matters. The facts can be sound while the process stays closed. What did the employee see that the form missed? What return path can both sides name?

The hardest split is development versus management. Coaching asks for honesty about habits and growth. Pay and role calls change the stakes. Mix them without naming the purpose, and people guard themselves. Split the purpose, and the ledger gets cleaner: learning in one line, decision in another.

You can use this without a title. Before you accept a score about your own task, ask what prior guidance it should summarize. Before you write a peer note, state the seen act and the effect, not a trait. When a formal cycle asks for a verdict, carry the earlier promise back into it. The process can name the debt without pretending the debt is harmless.

Limits: do not use this move to dodge real decisions. A score can be required. A role call can be due. A serious pattern may need a firm record even if past guidance was weak. When harm is active, act now; do not wait for a cleaner cycle. The move fails when it turns judgment into endless coaching, or when it uses dialogue to soften a decision that must be made.

examples.title: Score After the Chance
examples.scenario: The rating cycle has closed, and the trace runs backward to The Measurement Problem. A blue score box sits where the learning path should have been. The number was not false, but it narrowed the hour: Development Versus Management became one line. The move works only after a cost is paid. The person leaves with a rank first, then gets the behavior path that should have traveled earlier.
examples.whatToDo: Trace why the score narrowed attention before you rewrite the line. Keep the rating separate from the behavior path it must summarize.
examples.whyItMatters: Protect learning from the number, because a rank can settle the file while leaving the person unsure what behavior returns.

examples.title: Downstream Miss
examples.scenario: The downstream customer first feels the effect when the promised fix slips again. One stale coffee cup waits beside the support log. The Measurement Problem is visible: measurement counted the issue before Development Versus Management was separated. The miss is barely pulled back when guidance leaves the score sheet and returns to the task before the following handoff.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what the downstream miss proves. It proves the score traveled late, so move the behavior guidance back to the live task.
examples.whyItMatters: Answer the reader's question: the customer paid for delay because the process counted the issue before it guided the behavior.

examples.title: Complete Form, Thin Learning
examples.scenario: Measurement is quietly going wrong when every line in the cycle points to a rating and none points to learning. The form can be complete while guidance is thin. The Measurement Problem has not produced a blowup yet; it has narrowed attention. No one knows whether the following cycle will restore development or keep counting.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the score from the learning path. Write the rating in one place and the behavior that should return in another, then stop.
examples.whyItMatters: Count what the form hides. A clean rating can still leave no path, and the miss stays hidden until the same pattern comes back.

examples.title: Trait Line Crossed Out
examples.scenario: A manager drafting a review on Friday afternoon stops her pen after the word careless. The form's first line states the demand: no personality summary. She pulls the sentence back with SBI, to Situation, Behavior, and Impact; CORE adds Context, Observation, Result, and Explore. The move half-works. The evidence gets cleaner, but her first draft still treats Explore as a courtesy, not as shared ownership.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the trait. Replace it with the setting, the seen act, and the effect, then ask the employee what context changes the return path.
examples.whyItMatters: Keep the door open. Evidence without Explore can still become a verdict, even when every sentence sounds fair.

examples.title: The Process Enters Evidence
examples.scenario: Halfway through the rating write-up, the demand has already been made: inspect the formal performance review elements, not just the person. Bonus Chapter: A Radically Candid Performance Review asks whether those elements work and whether development conversations happen with everyone. The write-up starts blaming too narrowly until the process itself gets named as part of the evidence.
examples.whatToDo: Name what skipping this costs: the cycle blames a person for noise the process may have made. Inspect the element before you score the behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: Show the process in the ledger. A flawed form can block useful guidance, and fixing only the sentence leaves the same trap in place.

questions.prompt: A rating draft has a clear result but no employee voice. Which move best fits the evidence guidance?
choices: Use Context, Observation, and Result to ground the claim, then ask the employee to help shape the path forward.
Use the same evidence chain to make the verdict cleaner, then close the cycle before the employee adds context.
Hold the evidence until pay is settled, then use Explore only if the employee disputes the rating.
questions.explanation: CORE does not stop at a clean claim; Explore brings the employee into the return path. The tempting verdict-only choice keeps the process one-way.

questions.prompt: A score is accurate, yet the person leaves unsure what behavior should change. What best explains the miss?
choices: Measurement pulled attention toward the rating, so the learning path had to be protected from the number.
The score proved the lesson was complete, so adding behavior guidance would only reopen a settled management call after the fact.
The formal elements were too local, so the same rating template should replace the current process.
questions.explanation: The Measurement Problem is the split between counting and teaching. Treating the score as complete repeats the error the prose warns against.

questions.prompt: One proposed fix blames each weak write-up on the writer alone. Which principle does that break?
choices: It treats regular development talks as useful only after the formal cycle has closed and the person can no longer change.
It asks for behavior evidence before checking whether any score has been assigned.
It ignores that broken mechanics can distort guidance, so the process itself must be inspected.
questions.explanation: The bonus prompts ask whether current elements work. The writer-only answer is tempting, but it misses how design can block useful guidance.

questions.prompt: A company blends coaching notes and pay decisions into one undifferentiated hour. What happens downstream?
choices: People become more frank because the learning stakes and money stakes now share one path.
People treat every score as a development prompt, so the formal process needs fewer distinctions.
People guard themselves because coaching and management choices carry different stakes.
questions.explanation: Development talk and management calls need separate handling when pay or role force is present. The all-in-one answer sounds efficient, but it reduces honesty.

questions.prompt: Your sentence says someone is careless. Which replacement best follows the evidence rule?
choices: Keep the label but add that the pattern was visible in several moments across the cycle, so the trait sounds better supported.
Name the situation, the observed behavior, and the impact so the line points to something changeable.
Move the label into the score note, since personality language is clearer outside coaching.
questions.explanation: SBI turns a trait into observed evidence. The longer label choice still leaves the person with a hard-to-change summary.

questions.prompt: Before applying candor to a formal cycle at a new organization, what should you do first?
choices: Start from a universal template so the same standard travels cleanly across every process.
Inspect the actual elements in use, because the local process shapes how people behave.
Delay inspection until after the score is final, because candor belongs in the conversation.
questions.explanation: The prompts begin with the actual elements. A universal template is the near miss, because it assumes away the process that shapes behavior.

questions.prompt: A manager plans to run the formal review exactly like a weekly 1:1, since candor already flows in the everyday tools. What is the best correction?
choices: Keep the candor but respect the different job: the rating is recorded, so the hour summarizes the path instead of repeating a check-in.
Go ahead as planned, because strong everyday guidance already does the review's job and a separate practice adds nothing.
Flip the direction instead, giving each weekly 1:1 the weight of a rating so the formal hour needs nothing special.
questions.explanation: A formal review extends candor into a system that counts: the rating is recorded and decisions ride on it. The hour has its own job, summarizing guidance that already traveled while the record closes, so it is neither redundant nor a routine 1:1.

questions.prompt: An employee hears a major growth point for the first time during the rating hour. What should have happened earlier?
choices: The rating hour should have held the hard point until the score made it serious enough to act on with full attention.
Development talk should have happened regularly, so the formal cycle summarized instead of surprised.
The process should have waited for a second score before any behavior guidance traveled.
questions.explanation: Regular development talk is the guard against surprise. Waiting for the score is exactly the late move that removes the chance to change.

questions.prompt: Hard feedback was saved for the formal cycle, and trust drops after the conversation. Why?
choices: The evidence was too specific, so the person could not treat the rating as a broad enough verdict about the whole cycle.
The cycle included development language, so the person mistook a fair score for coaching.
The delayed guidance removed the chance to improve before evaluation, turning growth into a verdict.
questions.explanation: Surprise breaks trust because guidance arrived after it could help. The specific-evidence answer fails; specificity is useful when it arrives in time.

reviewCards.front: What should a formal cycle summarize?
reviewCards.back: Guidance that already traveled. If the hard point first appears there, the process has removed the chance to improve before evaluation.

reviewCards.front: Why can an accurate score still fail the person?
reviewCards.back: A score can pull attention toward rank and away from learning. Protect the behavior path so the number does not pose as development.

reviewCards.front: What does SBI add to evidence?
reviewCards.back: It ties the line to a situation, an observed behavior, and an impact. That makes the guidance easier to verify and change.

reviewCards.front: What does CORE add after the result?
reviewCards.back: Explore. The employee gets a say in context and the path ahead, so the cycle does not become a one-way verdict.

reviewCards.front: When should you inspect the process, not only the person?
reviewCards.back: When the formal elements may be shaping the behavior. A flawed process can distort guidance even when the writer tries to be candid.

reviewCards.front: What changes when candor enters the formal review?
reviewCards.back: The stakes rise: the score is recorded and management decisions ride on it. Candor still applies, but as a deliberate extension of the everyday tools, not a repeat of them.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Trace the Prior Guidance. Before a rating line stands, say what earlier guidance it records. If no earlier guidance exists, name that debt and move the behavior guidance back to the live task.

ifThenPlans.context: If a rating sentence surprises you
ifThenPlans.plan: If the surprise lands, then say aloud the guidance that should have arrived earlier.

ifThenPlans.context: If the score starts replacing the lesson
ifThenPlans.plan: If the number starts doing the talking, then say the behavior path in a separate sentence.

ifThenPlans.context: If the line describes a trait
ifThenPlans.plan: If a trait word appears, then say the seen behavior, the impact, and the employee's role in the path ahead.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Teach the move to one person in 10 minutes: say why a formal cycle should summarize prior guidance, then have them restate it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, measure one number: how many rating lines can point to prior guidance. If one cannot, say the missing guidance before the cycle closes.

memorableLines.text: A fair review can fail when the score lands after the chance to change.
Once a number is in play, the person being rated may stop hearing the lesson and start reading the odds.
The person who could have changed earlier pays first.
